title: Board Library for esp8266 2.5.0-beta2 does not work with WiFiClientSecure
body:
Hello Joel, just to let you know:
I recently upgraded the esp8266 board library to 2.5.0-beta2
Your library works for normal connections, but not for TLS using WiFiClientSecure, if the above mentioned board library is installed.

In the log of my mosquitto broker (on Raspberry Pi) I see, that the device is trying to connect:
`New connection from 192.168.11.84 on port 8883`
On the device  side, client.connect() never becomes true.
I tried to ignore this test and submitted a payload to a topic on the broker, it never arrived there.
It seems safe to assume, that the connection somehow is not correctly working

I downgraded to 2.4.2, everything is back to normal and working flawlessly.

From what I read on the github page of the ESP8266 project, they did a lot of work under the hood. Probably it is best to wait a few days or even weeks before digging into this, but this is up to you.

title: Keep Alive Overflow
body:
Hi again @256dpi .

I continue testing my project and I have noticed there is a "problem" when you set keep alive higher than 86 seconds. When I set keep alive with setOptions at 90 seconds, pingreq/pingresp cicle is done around 4 seconds delay. If I set it to 120 seconds, cicle is done around 25 seconds. If I set it to 85 seconds, works perfectly. I have been testing with UNO + Ethernet Shield with default millis() as clock source. 

What could be the reason?

Edit:
I have donwloaded 2.4.2 clean version and did same test. The result is the same.
comments:
[2019-02-01T09:04:45Z | 256dpi | comment]
It looks like this is caused by an integer overflow. Keep alive is a `uint16_t` that is multiplied by 750 to get 3/4 of the time in milliseconds. Now 87 * 750 is 65250 and right below 65536 which is the maximum of a `uint16_t`. I'll fix it ASAP.

[2019-02-08T12:59:23Z | 256dpi | comment]
I released a new version that hopefully fixed the bug. Would you be able to test it?

[2019-02-08T22:17:18Z | jmpmscorp | comment]
I have been testing new release with UNO + ETHERNET SHIELD with two different values, 150 and 300 seconds. I can confirm that this bug is resolved.

Thanks again @256dpi.

title: Exceeding length crashes devices
body:
If I exceed the max length of the MQTT packet, I expect to get some sort of failure.  Instead, on ESP8266 at least, I get a system crash.  I can't see any way of doing this without changing the API unless you simply ignore overly long messages.

This is possibly a bug in paho embedded of course, I'm having a bit of a hard time finding who's entirely responsible.
comments:
[2015-12-29T18:31:36Z | 256dpi | comment]
Publishing too long messages should be safe as it is checked here: https://github.com/256dpi/arduino-mqtt/blob/master/src/lib/MQTTSerializePublish.c#L62. But receiving too long messages will crash the application as there are no checks implemented yet: https://github.com/256dpi/arduino-mqtt/blob/master/src/lib/MQTTDeserializePublish.c#L35. Sadly, this is a limitation of the paho embedded library.

I'll look into this but it might be complicated to resolve quickly.

[2017-05-03T12:29:59Z | 256dpi | comment]
This has been fixed in #59. The code will return false on `yield()` if the receive buffer is too small.

title: Error in temperature and brightness when using lightOperation
body:
Only tested on "TRADFRI bulb E27 WS opal 980lm" with firmware 1.2.217 (Gateway firmware is 1.2.42).

To reproduce, first set the brightness of the light with

```javascript
client.operateLight(light, {"dimmer":3})
```

When inspecting `light` it will have its `dimmer` property set to 4. Likewise, 
```javascript
client.operateLight(light, {"colorTemperature":100})
```
will result in a `colorTemperature` of 98 in the light object.

There are several more values that will not get set correctly in similar fashion. I suppose this is due to conversion between values used by the gateway and the [0,100] scale used in the API.

It would be great if the proper ranges for both brightness and temperature were usable in the API, since it allows finer granularity control. You probably already know this but:
   - brightness (property 5851) accepts values in [0,254]
   - color temperature (property 5711) accepts any value but WS bulbs will show values in [250, 454]. CWS bulbs supposedly can't use this property but I wouldn't know since I don't own any.

title: Causes crashes in OctoPrint's login when disabled
body:
I just had a user report an odd issue in foosel/OctoPrint#2442. They have the Astroprint plugin disabled, and that makes them not able to login anymore.

A closer look at OctoPrint's plugin subsystem reveals that contrary to what I so far assumed, plugins are still loaded even when disabled. Which means that in your case the plugin's implementation will be initialized, and in its constructor functions will be attached to Flask Login's loggedIn and loggedOut signals that try to send messages to the frontend via `self._plugin_manager` - however, if your plugin is disabled, your plugin won't be fully initialized, `self._plugin_manager` hence not injected and that means things crash inside Flask Login when trying to call your signal handler and the login fails with an HTTP 500.

I'll have to do something about this on OctoPrint's side, however I strongly suggest to not attach any stuff to the system as long as the plugin is not fully initialized (read: the `initialized` method on it is called). 

Could you fix this on your end? As I said, I'll also look into finding a good fix on mine. If push comes to shove, disabled plugins will simply get the same treatment that blacklisted ones get, meaning some metadata will be missing in the plugin list but no code will be executed at all, preventing such issues in the future.

> SRS_IOTHUBCLIENT_41_003 [ If the value of OPTION_DO_WORK_FREQUENCY_IN_MS is greater than 100, IotHubClientCore_SetOption shall return IOTHUB_CLIENT_INVALID_ARG ]
SRS_IOTHUBCLIENT_41_004 [ If currentMessageTimeout is not greater than do_work_freq_ms, IotHubClientCore_SetOption shall return IOTHUB_CLIENT_INVALID_ARG ]

That sounds good.  There is also a case where the currentMessageTimeout is set on the iotHubClientInstance, even if the value is less than do_work_freq_ms. I think we should not set it on the handle in that case.

[2019-05-21T18:38:44Z | YoDaMa | comment]
Just adding here. The uint16_t vs. tickcounter_ms_t is intentional. The documentation should be updated to indicate that tickcounter_ms_t is the necessary unit from the API side for setting this variable. It can also be added to the convenience sample to indicate the proper usage of this variable.

Your analysis on the code is good though (really, a great issue file with good code snippet and everything! Thanks!). Here's a deeper explanation:

**Why use `tickcounter_ms_t` for OPTION_DO_WORK_FREQUENCY_IN_MS?**
- In `iothub_client_core.c` the OPTION_DO_WORK_FREQUENCY_IN_MS has a value that is checked against `iotHubClientInstance->currentMessageTimeout`, which is of type `tickcounter_ms_t` (which is defined in the azure_c_shared_utilities as `uint_fast64_t` or `uint_fast32_t` depending on the platform). 
- Because of this check against `currentMessageTimeout`, OPTION_DO_WORK_FREQUENCY_IN_MS needs to be of a type `tickcounter_ms_t *`. 

**But then in `iothub_client_core.c`, `do_work_freq_ms` is set as a `uint16_t`. Why?**
- `do_work_freq_ms` is used to specify a sleep interval via `ThreadAPI_Sleep`, which takes a type `unsigned int`. 
- If the `do_work_freq_ms` were a `tickcounter_ms_t`, we end up with a bug. When it is cast to a `unsigned int` to input into `ThreadAPI_Sleep`, the number will be undefined (just random garbage). 
- So to avoid this we cast the `tickcounter_ms_t` pointer to a `uint16_t` pointer, and because we've set the range to be between 0-100, there's no chance of this pointer cast losing data. The `do_work_freq_ms` variable for `iotHubClientInstance` will be set as the dereferenced `uint16_t` pointer.

[2019-05-21T21:43:41Z | massand | comment]
@kiranpradeep - @YoDaMa brings up valid points - the API is correct infact. 
The data type for SetOption cannot truly be validated in our C SDK, but it should really be tickcounter_ms_t (in line with the OPTION_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT). The internal version is uint16_t to ensure we don't recast the option value for the ThreadAPI_Sleep(unsigned int) call. 
So, your sample should contain this - 
```
tickcounter_ms_t timeout = 10000;
int ret = IoTHubDeviceClient_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, OPTION_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT, &timeout);
assert(ret == IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK);

tickcounter_ms_t sleepTime = 100; //assuming data type from declarations - is this correct ?
ret = IoTHubDeviceClient_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, OPTION_DO_WORK_FREQUENCY_IN_MS, &sleepTime);
assert(ret == IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK);
```
Improvements that @YoDaMa is working on his PR are:
1) Switching our internal data type for do_work from uint16_t to unsigned int - because ThreadAPI_Sleep(unsigned int) uses that type and we want to be consistent
2) Adding unit tests to validate some additional scenarios - comparison with messageTimeout, range checks.
3) Adding convenience sample usage (he started this already in PR above)

Please help review the work when he is done, so we are sure it works for you. Thanks!

body:
**Development Machine, OS, Compiler (and Other Relevant Toolchain Info)**

Ubuntu 16.04

**SDK Version (Please Give Commit SHA if Manually Compiling)**

Release 2019-05-16

**Protocol**

AMQP

**Describe the Bug**

Hi,

the application I am building is supposed to establish an IoT Hub connection when it is needed and close it after a certain timeout when there are no new messages and after all messages in the queue have been sent (IoTHubDeviceClient_LL_GetSendStatus() returns IOTHUB_CLIENT_SEND_STATUS_IDLE).

As a measure against losing messages when the network goes down, I am resending messages in the confirm callback if the result is IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT or IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_ERROR.

If the connection stays down long enough for the SDK to run into a timeout and start attempts to reestablish the AMQP connection, the confirm callback is called with result IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_ERROR. Sending the message again now via IoTHubDeviceClient_LL_SendEventAsync() returns IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK, but IoTHubDeviceClient_LL_GetSendStatus() returns IOTHUB_CLIENT_SEND_STATUS_IDLE.

If the IoT Hub client is destroyed now because my application assumes that there are no pending messages, the confirm callback for the message that has just been put into the queue is called with result IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_BECAUSE_DESTROY.

I would expect IoTHubDeviceClient_LL_GetSendStatus() to return IOTHUB_CLIENT_SEND_STATUS_BUSY as long as there are messages waiting to be sent, no matter if they were enqueued while the transport is connected or not.
Or is there a different official way to find out if there are any pending messages in the queue?

EDIT: The behavior does not occur with the MQTT transport

title: IoTHubDeviceClient_SendReportedState / IoTHubDeviceClient_SendEventAsync only allows one callback for all reports
body:
(Note that below applies to `IoTHubDeviceClient_SendEventAsync` as well by analogy)

When invoking `IoTHubDeviceClient_SendReportedState` (or its module cousin), we only record the last callback function.

Consider for example

```c
IoTHubClientCore_SendReportedState(handle, "state-data-1",..., callback1);
IoTHubClientCore_SendReportedState(handle, "state-data-2",..., callback2);
```

`IoTHubClientCore_SendReportedState` (which does all the work) is saving the callback function at a handle-wide level, namely
```c
iotHubClientInstance->reported_state_callback = reportedStateCallback;
```

This makes the code above not work, because the `callback2` will end up over-writing `callback1` in the per-handle.  While this is OK for stuff like taking incoming device methods and properties to just have 1 dispatcher per handle, for device initiated sending there maybe legit reasons for having different callbacks for different types of reported properties / telemetry.

Note that the `LL` layer does this correctly - it tracks the callback function per the context (e.g. `IOTHUB_DEVICE_TWIN`) that is created per sending property.

title: AMQP <-> Eventhub <-> C SDK <-> C# SDK system properties mismatch
body:
I have noticed a couple of mismatches in behavior as well as interface between the different SDKs and the IoT Hub documentation.

If you take a look at the [documentation for messages](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/iot-hub/iot-hub-devguide-messaging#message-format) you can see that a message should have fields `To` and `UserId`. From the client side, the `To` field isn't necessary since it's implicitly defined as the corresponding IoTHub. The `UserId` field, should be defined as far as I understand it.

Furthermore, the [C# SDKs Message Class](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.azure.devices.client.message?view=azuredevicesclient-1.2.6) allows me to set both fields. The [C SDKs equivalent](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/master/iothub_client/inc/iothub_message.h), as far as I know, is not able to set either field. I can see why there is no method for the `To` property, but there should be one for the `UserId` property, even if it should be the same as the DeviceId.

When I receive a message from the C SDK with the [C# EventData Class](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.servicebus.messaging.eventdata?view=azureservicebus-4.0.0) and take a look at the system properties, both fields are missing. This is unexpected, because the documentation as well as the [AMQP Protocol](http://www.amqp.org/sites/amqp.org/files/amqp.pdf) Chapter 3.2 let me believe that both fields should exist.

On the other hand, in the [C SDKs EventData class](https://github.com/Azure/azure-event-hubs-c/blob/master/eventhub_client/inc/eventdata.h) does not even provide me with a way to access system properties like the C# SDK does.

I have also discussed this issue on [stackoverflow ](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/43200966/how-do-i-set-certain-system-properties-with-the-azure-iot-c-sdk-for-the-amqp-pro) with Rita Han - MSFT, who proposed a workaround solution by setting the `To` and `UserId` properties via the application properties instead of the system / message properties.

So I wonder:

- Is this mismatch between the APIs and behaviors intentional?
- Is there some "proper" way of setting those properties with the C SDK?
- What is the actual semantic of `UserId` and when should it be set?
- Is this an issue with the C SDK? If so, is it going to be fixed?

Kind Regards,
Christopher Czyba

[2017-07-03T17:28:43Z | chrit-msft | comment]
@czyba I have discussed this issue with the C SDK owner and would like to answer the 4 questions you posted above. 

•Is this mismatch between the APIs and behaviors intentional?
Behavior should be aligned between the SDKs and this is being investigated.

•Is there some "proper" way of setting those properties with the C SDK?
The system uses these and sets them properly.
If you are attempting to identify the origin of the device sending the message use the Device Connection ID.
If you need your own custom way of identifing message origin you can use the application properties as indicated in the information provided on stackoverflow.

•What is the actual semantic of  UserId  and when should it be set?
UserID is used in the cloud to device message by the system and it is not
intended to be set by the user in a device to cloud message.

•Is this an issue with the C SDK? If so, is it going to be fixed?
No it isn't an issue with C SDK.  The C# SDK incorrectly exposes these system properties.  The SDK Teams are working on aligning the SDKs.

Please let me know if this sufficiently answers your questions.

title: Reported twin info can enter no-free state on MQTT
body:
Acknowledgements to @markrad who did great investigation here and whose issue I'm basically copy/pasting below.

I've put a preliminary fix up https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/tree/mqtt-twin-timeout-cleanup.  Cleaned up some of code so it's more common and of course removing reported properties.  UT's are passing but we clearly need more to cover this case.  I'll create PR after I sleep on this some and get UT.

--
Each time a device twin packet is sent to the IoT hub, the SDK will queue an item to the list ack_waiting_queue in iothubtransport_mqtt_common.c. This item will remain on the queue until the IoT hub sends a acknowledgment for the twin update.

At issue though is if there's a network disconnect (and I believe specifically that MQTT layer hasn't been alerted by underlying network stack) these packets have never been sent. Since these ack items do not have any kind of time out mechanism they will continue to collect on the ack queue and will never been removed.

There is a function in iothubtransport_mqtt_common.c called removeExpiredGetTwinRequestPendingAck that will clear the ack_waiting_queue of expired items but it specifically only processes items that are flagged as RETRIEVE_PROPERTIES. The end result is that the ack_waiting_queue will continue to grow every time there is a failure of the connection to the IoT hub.

title: PnP Environmental sensor does not follow HTTP status code conventions
body:
Our environmental sensor PnP sample interface today has an async command as part of its DTDL.

The way the code works:
* Returns a 202 on the initial acceptance of the request.
* A second later sends another 202 back indicating request is in progress.
* A second later sends a 200 to show the request is done.

The subsequent send of the 202 is not correct per my reading of HTTP status codes and some discussions.  We need instead to return a 102 to show processing on step2 above.

See https://httpstatuses.com/202 and https://httpstatuses.com/102.

title: PnP should provide reported properties to app always
body:
Currently for C SDK, when we get a full twin we report properties to application *only* if there are desired properties in the list.  If there is a reported property but not a desired property, we just swallow it.

This isn't right.  We should always provide reported properties.  This will help bandwidth conscious interfaces to be thoughtful about whether they report back a given reported property again or whether they realize the server has what they were going to send up anyway and save the round-trip.

title: IoTHubClient_LL_SendEventAsync/IoTHubMessage_Destroy - memory management and example consistency
body:
The question is when is it safe to destroy the message - call IoTHubMessage_Destroy?

E.g. the following code immediately calls Destroy after SendEventAsync - which seems strange to me, because of the asynchronous character!? So couldn't it be that the message is freed before it is even sent?

https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/241b66eb6499e2c019682f252d911ef2b28d1302/iothub_client/samples/iothub_ll_client_sample_amqp_shared/iothub_ll_client_sample_amqp_shared.c#L283-L297

Also other code - like...

https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/241b66eb6499e2c019682f252d911ef2b28d1302/iothub_client/samples/iothub_client_sample_module_filter/iothub_client_sample_module_filter.c#L151-L154

https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/241b66eb6499e2c019682f252d911ef2b28d1302/iothub_client/samples/iothub_client_sample_module_filter/iothub_client_sample_module_filter.c#L86-L91

only destroys the message if the call to SendEventAsync fails - and otherwise postpones the disposal into the confirmation callback - this seems logically more correct. But if this is correct, then there is the bonus question - what happens if the callback is NULL - is the message freed implicitly by SendEventAsync in this case? Or are we just having a memory leak since there is no defined event at which we can be sure it is ok to dispose the sent messages?

Unfortunately the documentation (https://docs.microsoft.com/de-de/azure/iot-hub/iot-c-sdk-ref/iothub-client-core-ll-h/iothubclientcore-ll-sendeventasync) is just not meaningful and the sample code is as explained contradictive.

Thanks in advance for any hints and please don't hesitate to ask if I kept to short and you need additional input to get the intention.
comments:
[2019-11-12T17:12:33Z | ewertons | comment]
Hi @alaendle ,
we apologize for the documentation not being straightforward about that aspect. Indeed we are constantly reviewing and updating our docs, but some information might still be missing.

Answering your question, IoTHubClient_LL_SendEventAsync, IoTHubDeviceClient_LL_SendEventAsync and IoTHubDeviceClient_SendEventAsync all create an internal copy of the IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE instance provided as argument.
That is why you can destroy the message right after calling any of these functions above.
The internal copy is then owned by the IoT Hub client layer, that destroys the message as soon as it is effectively sent out on the wire to the Azure IoT Hub.

title: Don't directly reference `DIGITALTWIN_CLIENT_SDK_VERSION` in SDK Information
body:
PnP's sample of SDKInformation has a hardcoded reference of `DIGITALTWIN_CLIENT_SDK_VERSION` in it to specify the version.

If the dev updates the SDK and statically links the code in, then we'll be fine because `DIGITALTWIN_CLIENT_SDK_VERSION` will be updated and they'll recompile.

If they're using pnp_sdk.dll and not recompiling, directly referencing `DIGITALTWIN_CLIENT_SDK_VERSION` is a problem.

Instead we should:
* Fix SDKInformation to use `DigitalTwin_Client_GetVersionString`.
* Remove `DIGITALTWIN_CLIENT_SDK_VERSION` from the header so that other people don't make the same mistake.

title: AV in IoTHub client when reconnecting on AMQP
body:
<!--

- **SDK version used:** <VERSION> <!-- Please include the SDK version -->
4b9b17fb45a04c79e271c54a09bad2b12b19a9b3

# Description of the issue:
<!-- Please be as detailed as possible: which feature has a problem, how often does it fail,  -->
I setup a client sending to IoTHub continuously every 1 second by modifying iothub_client_sample_amqp.c to send every 1s.
Then I blocked traffic from the server to the client by specific means until the reconnect was triggered.
At the reconnect time => AV.

# Code sample exhibiting the issue:
<!-- Please remove any connection string information! -->

// Copyright (c) Microsoft. All rights reserved.
// Licensed under the MIT license. See LICENSE file in the project root for full license information.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#include "azure_c_shared_utility/platform.h"
#include "azure_c_shared_utility/threadapi.h"
#include "azure_c_shared_utility/crt_abstractions.h"
#include "iothub_client.h"
#include "iothub_message.h"
#include "iothubtransportamqp.h"

#ifdef MBED_BUILD_TIMESTAMP
#include "certs.h"
#endif // MBED_BUILD_TIMESTAMP

/*String containing Hostname, Device Id & Device Key in the format:                         */
/*  "HostName=<host_name>;DeviceId=<device_id>;SharedAccessKey=[REDACTED_HIGH_CONFIDENCE_SECRET:azure_iot_shared_access_key]"                */
/*  "HostName=<host_name>;DeviceId=<device_id>;SharedAccessSignature=<device_sas_token>"    */
static const char* connectionString = "hagauaga, insert your credentials here, blah";

static int callbackCounter;
static bool g_continueRunning;
static char msgText[1024];
static char propText[1024];
#define MESSAGE_COUNT       50000
#define DOWORK_LOOP_NUM     3

typedef struct EVENT_INSTANCE_TAG
{
    IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE messageHandle;
    size_t messageTrackingId;  // For tracking the messages within the user callback.
} EVENT_INSTANCE;

static IOTHUBMESSAGE_DISPOSITION_RESULT ReceiveMessageCallback(IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE message, void* userContextCallback)
{
    int* counter = (int*)userContextCallback;
    const unsigned char* buffer = NULL;
    size_t size = 0;
    const char* messageId;
    const char* correlationId;

    // Message properties
    if ((messageId = IoTHubMessage_GetMessageId(message)) == NULL)
    {
        messageId = "<null>";
    }

    if ((correlationId = IoTHubMessage_GetCorrelationId(message)) == NULL)
    {
        correlationId = "<null>";
    }

    // Message content
    IOTHUBMESSAGE_CONTENT_TYPE contentType = IoTHubMessage_GetContentType(message);

    if (contentType == IOTHUBMESSAGE_BYTEARRAY)
    {
        if (IoTHubMessage_GetByteArray(message, &buffer, &size) == IOTHUB_MESSAGE_OK)
        {
            (void)printf("Received Message [%d]\r\n Message ID: %s\r\n Correlation ID: %s\r\n BINARY Data: <<<%.*s>>> & Size=%d\r\n", *counter, messageId, correlationId, (int)size, buffer, (int)size);
        }
        else
        {
            (void)printf("Failed getting the BINARY body of the message received.\r\n");
        }
    }
    else if (contentType == IOTHUBMESSAGE_STRING)
    {
        if ((buffer = (const unsigned char*)IoTHubMessage_GetString(message)) != NULL && (size = strlen((const char*)buffer)) > 0)
        {
            (void)printf("Received Message [%d]\r\n Message ID: %s\r\n Correlation ID: %s\r\n STRING Data: <<<%.*s>>> & Size=%d\r\n", *counter, messageId, correlationId, (int)size, buffer, (int)size);

            // If we receive the work 'quit' then we stop running
        }
        else
        {
            (void)printf("Failed getting the STRING body of the message received.\r\n");
        }
    }
    else
    {
        (void)printf("Failed getting the body of the message received (type %i).\r\n", contentType);
    }

    // Retrieve properties from the message
    MAP_HANDLE mapProperties = IoTHubMessage_Properties(message);
    if (mapProperties != NULL)
    {
        const char*const* keys;
        const char*const* values;
        size_t propertyCount = 0;
        if (Map_GetInternals(mapProperties, &keys, &values, &propertyCount) == MAP_OK)
        {
            if (propertyCount > 0)
            {
                size_t index;

                printf(" Message Properties:\r\n");
                for (index = 0; index < propertyCount; index++)
                {
                    printf("\tKey: %s Value: %s\r\n", keys[index], values[index]);
                }
                printf("\r\n");
            }
        }
    }

    if (size == (strlen("quit") * sizeof(char)) && memcmp(buffer, "quit", size) == 0)
    {
        g_continueRunning = false;
    }

    /* Some device specific action code goes here... */
    (*counter)++;
    return IOTHUBMESSAGE_ACCEPTED;
}

static void SendConfirmationCallback(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_RESULT result, void* userContextCallback)
{
    EVENT_INSTANCE* eventInstance = (EVENT_INSTANCE*)userContextCallback;
    (void)printf("Confirmation[%d] received for message tracking id = %zu with result = %s\r\n", callbackCounter, eventInstance->messageTrackingId, ENUM_TO_STRING(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_RESULT, result));
    /* Some device specific action code goes here... */
    callbackCounter++;
    IoTHubMessage_Destroy(eventInstance->messageHandle);
}

void iothub_client_sample_amqp_run(void)
{
    IOTHUB_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE iotHubClientHandle;

    EVENT_INSTANCE messages[MESSAGE_COUNT];

    g_continueRunning = true;
    srand((unsigned int)time(NULL));
    double avgWindSpeed = 10.0;

    callbackCounter = 0;
    int receiveContext = 0;

    (void)printf("Starting the IoTHub client sample AMQP...\r\n");

    if (platform_init() != 0)
    {
        printf("Failed to initialize the platform.\r\n");
    }
    else
    {
        if ((iotHubClientHandle = IoTHubClient_LL_CreateFromConnectionString(connectionString, AMQP_Protocol)) == NULL)
        {
            (void)printf("ERROR: iotHubClientHandle is NULL!\r\n");
        }
        else
        {
            bool traceOn = true;
            IoTHubClient_LL_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, "logtrace", &traceOn);

#ifdef MBED_BUILD_TIMESTAMP
            // For mbed add the certificate information
            if (IoTHubClient_LL_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, "TrustedCerts", certificates) != IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK)
            {
                printf("failure to set option \"TrustedCerts\"\r\n");
            }
#endif // MBED_BUILD_TIMESTAMP

            /* Setting Message call back, so we can receive Commands. */
            if (IoTHubClient_LL_SetMessageCallback(iotHubClientHandle, ReceiveMessageCallback, &receiveContext) != IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK)
            {
                (void)printf("ERROR: IoTHubClient_SetMessageCallback..........FAILED!\r\n");
            }
            else
            {
                (void)printf("IoTHubClient_SetMessageCallback...successful.\r\n");

                /* Now that we are ready to receive commands, let's send some messages */
                size_t iterator = 0;
                size_t counter = 0;
                do
                {
                    counter++;

                    if (counter % 1000 == 0)
                    {
                        iterator++;
                        if (iterator < MESSAGE_COUNT)
                        {
                            sprintf_s(msgText, sizeof(msgText), "{\"deviceId\":\"myFirstDevice\",\"windSpeed\":%.2f}", avgWindSpeed + (rand() % 4 + 2));
                            if ((messages[iterator].messageHandle = IoTHubMessage_CreateFromByteArray((const unsigned char*)msgText, strlen(msgText))) == NULL)
                            {
                                (void)printf("ERROR: iotHubMessageHandle is NULL!\r\n");
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                messages[iterator].messageTrackingId = iterator;

                                MAP_HANDLE propMap = IoTHubMessage_Properties(messages[iterator].messageHandle);
                                (void)sprintf_s(propText, sizeof(propText), "PropMsg_%zu", iterator);
                                if (Map_AddOrUpdate(propMap, "PropName", propText) != MAP_OK)
                                {
                                    (void)printf("ERROR: Map_AddOrUpdate Failed!\r\n");
                                }

                                if (IoTHubClient_LL_SendEventAsync(iotHubClientHandle, messages[iterator].messageHandle, SendConfirmationCallback, &messages[iterator]) != IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK)
                                {
                                    (void)printf("ERROR: IoTHubClient_SendEventAsync..........FAILED!\r\n");
                                }
                                else
                                {
                                    (void)printf("IoTHubClient_SendEventAsync accepted data for transmission to IoT Hub.\r\n");
                                }
                            }
                        }
                    }

                    IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork(iotHubClientHandle);
                    ThreadAPI_Sleep(1);
                } while (g_continueRunning);

                (void)printf("iothub_client_sample_amqp has gotten quit message, call DoWork %d more time to complete final sending...\r\n", DOWORK_LOOP_NUM);
                for (size_t index = 0; index < DOWORK_LOOP_NUM; index++)
                {
                    IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork(iotHubClientHandle);
                    ThreadAPI_Sleep(1);
                }
            }
            IoTHubClient_LL_Destroy(iotHubClientHandle);
        }
        platform_deinit();
    }
}

int main(void)
{
    iothub_client_sample_amqp_run();
    return 0;
}

[2017-07-06T12:53:21Z | AndWass | comment]
Found a fix you might want to try as well.

In message_sender.c in function on_link_state_changed a call will be made to the function `indicate_all_messages_as_error`. This function frees all the messages and their associated memory. After this (a little while on) `on_session_state_changed` (in link.c) will be called with the new state set to SESSION_STATE_ERROR. This will call `remove_all_pending_deliveries` which will loop through all pending deliveries and call the `on_delivery_settled callback`. This callback will then touch and attempt to use the previously freed memory and finally also free the message again.

Simply removing all calls to `indicate_all_messages_as_error` in `on_link_state_change` (around lines 560 in message_sender.c in uamqp) will make the crashing go away but I don't know if this causes other problems though.

title: UploadBlob Timeout is arbitrarily set to 242 seconds.

I noticed that the uploadToBlob functionality has an arbitrarily set timeout for Debian Jessie and probably other linux with curl based systems. After investigating where the timeout came from I noticed that [httpapi_curl](https://github.com/Azure/azure-c-shared-utility/blob/bad7ead6cd73fe9e1d95ca0fe812a1e9b4e2a601/adapters/httpapi_curl.c#L124) Sets the timeout to an arbitrary 242s. 

However, I tried to upload a 20MB file over a mobile connection with a roughly 50kB/s upload. Thus I  require to have at least a timeout of 400s. 

Is there some way to achieve this?
Would it be possible to add a method which allows setting the timeout or disabling it altogether?

Kind Regards,
Christopher Czyba

title: IoTHubClient_UploadToBlobAsync blocks the whole iothub
body:
Hello Azure SDK Team,

I have noticed that the method `IoTHubClient_UploadToBlobAsync` completely blocks any operation of the iothub. This results in messages not being sent in parallel with a potentially long lasting upload.

According to comment in [iothub_client.c source](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/master/iothub_client/src/iothub_client.c#L1760) this actually needn't be. Would it be possible to remove the lock and allow sends to be happen in parallel. It would also be possible to extent the method by using a "file upload" queue as well.

Otherwise I would recommend adjusting the documentation accordingly.

Kind Regards,
Christopher Czyba
comments:
[2017-08-07T15:42:47Z | ewertons | comment]
hi @czyba ,
thanks for your comment.

I checked the code and it locks only to start a new Thread, then unlocks right away.
I'm checking the rest of the code, but just to confirm: are you experiencing the block or you are concluding there is a block based on the function is written?

[2017-08-08T05:43:15Z | czyba | comment]
Hi @ewertons,

I noticed this issue because I actually experienced the block in a program. Afterwards I checked the code to find out why it actually occurs. As far as I can see it is roughly because of this:

1. As you said, `IoTHubClient_UploadToBlobAsync` only blocks in order to create the thread. And indeed, that does not seem to be the issue.
2. The thread however runs the `uploadingThread` function, which in turn calls `Lock(savedData->iotHubClientHandle->LockHandle)`. During the period when the lock is being held `IoTHubClient_LL_UploadToBlob(savedData->iotHubClientHandle->IoTHubClientLLHandle, savedData->destinationFileName, savedData->source, savedData->size)` is called, which is a blocking call.
3. The `ScheduleWork_Thread` tries to lock the IoTHub before sending messages. Since the file upload still holds the lock for some time no message will be sent until the file upload is completed or aborted.

Furthermore since nearly all methods require to lock the IoTHub, so suddenly the async non-blocking calls and all other "immediate" calls will result in blocking operations. I have modified and attached the
[iothub_client_sample_upload_to_blob.c](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/files/1206998/iothub_client_sample_upload_to_blob_c.txt) sample such that it exhibits said behavior. In my sample I have used SetRetryPolicy for simplicity sake, but the issue occurs with nearly all functions.

This also results in the IoTHub not being destroyed, since the file upload is not interrupted. Thus it may happen that a program may not terminate immediately but just in a couple of seconds if a file upload is in progress. I hope this showcases my issues.

Kind Regards,
Christopher Czyba

title: [MQTT] ConnectionStatus / EventConfirmation callback behaviors are not consistent when network is disconnected
body:
In the release of "2016-11-17", when running the test cases to disconnect/resume network, the callback behaviors could be different, hence making the program to use Azure IoT device SDK become difficult to manage network situations.

Usually we expect "ConnectionStatus" callback will report connection status once the connection status is changed. However when disconnect/resume network manually, we'll found it's not true always. If the program starts with network disconnected, "ConnectionStatus" callback might not be called, and this might happened maybe 7 times out of 10 tries, and there are 3 times the ConnectionStatus callback will be called when doing the first call to "IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork()". This kind of behavior make it difficult to detect network disconnection, if the program is waiting for C2D message from IoT Hub.

"EventConfirmation" callback for "IoTHubClient_LL_SendEventAsync()" is also inconsistent. If the network disconnection is detected during the time trying to send the message, "EventConfirmation" will get a error callback, and this message is then aborted/dropped, hence a message level retry could be handled within this callback. If network is not resumed, then for the next message, "EventConfirmation" callback will never be called (if "messageTimeout" is not set) to reflect network error.

So the message sent callback might have two different result in corresponding to network disconnection, one is callback with error, the other is no callback or a callback with timeout error.

Please help to make the behavior consistent, so to avoid potential defects.

[2017-01-20T00:45:01Z | BertKleewein | comment]
Regarding the connection status callback, I have a fix in  progress.  

Regarding the second issue: 
> So the message sent callback might have two different result in corresponding to network disconnection, one is callback with error, the other is no callback or a callback with timeout error.

It appears that we have a timing issue here.  Our SDK will queue messages if the network is not available.  We have a retry policy in place which will try to reconnect to the service with an exponential backoff.  If the SDK is not able to connect. it will retain the message in its queue until a connection can acquired or the timeout period expires.

The timing issue is that a network disconnection that happens in the middle of sending a message will cause a failure to be returned to the client.

In this way, you get an inconsistent behavior depending on the timing of the disconnect.  Most of the time, lack of a network connection will cause the message to be queued.  If you happen to hit a disconnect window, where the disconnection event takes place while the SDK is in the middle of sending a message, then that message will be aborted.  This is by design because the SDK only knows that a network error has taken place while sending the message.  It does not know what caused that error.  Since it's possible that the contents of the message caused the network error, it is better to return failure to the caller rather than re-queue the (possibly harmful) message and risk another network errror.

If you would like to introduce consistency by causing your messages to "fail quickly" when the network is not available, you should be able to set a short timeout as follows:
```
            tickcounter_ms_t timeout = 5000;
            IoTHubClient_LL_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, "messageTimeout", &timeout);
```

Regarding the second problem, I hope I was able to provide sufficient explanation and maybe some workarounds. - **OS and version used:** Linux OpenWrt 3.18.29 mips GNU/Linux <!-- Windows 10, Ubuntu 15.04... -->

# Description of the issue:
I've updated to latest Azure IoT SDK on my device from 1.1.14 to 1.1.21 and experienced the following issue: it looks like IoT Hub SDK for C is unable to reconnect after connection loss over MQTT protocol, for example, when it loses Internet access.  

For instance, if SDK loses connection to Azure servers due to Internet connection problem, when Internet access is back again, it cannot establish a connection to servers -- SDK returns `IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_DEVICE_DISABLED` as a connection status. Also, it keeps trying to reconnect, but with no success. 

I'm using x509 authentification, 60s MQTT keepAlive ping and `IOTHUB_CLIENT_RETRY_INTERVAL` retry policy without a maximum limit. The device is connected to the internet over Wi-Fi. It sends JSON messages and updates properties using device twin.

[2017-10-10T16:12:20Z | ewertons | comment]
@kiranpradeep , this is a good additional piece of information.
So it doesn't mean that you don't get reconnected at all, it means it takes a lot of time to reconnect?

Are you aware that the IoTHubClient has a feature called Retry Policy? The default retry policy is EXPONENTIAL_BACKOFF_WITH_JITTER. It means that if there is a disconnection, the client will retry connecting within 1 second, then 2 secs, 4, 8, ... eventually taking a long time (hours) if the connection has been disrupted for too long. 
The exponential retry policy is not recommended for connections that stay offline for too long (several minutes). 

You can control the retry policy by using this [API function](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/master/iothub_client/inc/iothub_client_ll.h#L375).

Could you try setting it to a more aggressive retry policy (IOTHUB_CLIENT_RETRY_INTERVAL or IOTHUB_CLIENT_RETRY_IMMEDIATE) and see if the issue gets resolved?

Hi there! thank you for discovering and submitting an issue!

- **SDK version used:** 1.1.21

title: No reconnection after network disconnection
body:
Hi,

I'm facing the some problems with the connection to the IoTHub after connection lose.

## Setup
I'm running the last version of the SDK `2017-10-09` on Ubuntu 16.04.
Ubuntu is running on a VM on a Windows 10.

## Description 

I'm running a simple client that send every 5 seconds a message on the IoTHub.
The transport protocol used is MQTT.

### Case 1 (working)
When the device is disconnected "locally" (see schema below) the SDK handles the reconnection properly after some time when the connection is back. The messages are correctly enqueued and are sent as soon as the connection is back.
`|device|---------|Ubuntu(VM)|----X----|Windows|---------|Internet|---------|IoTHub|`

### Case 2 (not working)
When the device is disconnected from windows (we cut the connection), The socket in the SDK receive a signal 13 (SIGPIPE) and the connection is not recovered.
`|device|---------|Ubuntu(VM)|---------|Windows|----X----|Internet|---------|IoTHub|`


In fact, we observed the same behavior on a real device, when the internet connection is lost by a switch. 
`|device|---------|switch|----X----|Internet|---------|IoTHub|`

First thanks to everyone for repro steps & my apologies that this has lingered so long.

**;tl-dr.  We have a provisional fix, look for it sometime next week.  It will make the 3/30 release.**

Because I'm guessing the audience here is geeks and wants the details...

MQTT_WS on reconnection is not properly blasting the tlsio_* layer and there's cached gunk lying around that we pass to openssl, schannel (this repros on Windows).  AMQP_WS in fact does clean up after itself which is why this bug doesn't repro on it.

I've put in a proof of concept in MQTT where its much more aggressive cleaning up its lower layer.  It's working very well in smoke tests; I've killed proxy ~10 times across varying lengths of timeouts and MQTT_WS always returns.  On both Windows 10 and Ubuntu 16.04.

Even though this is like a 2 liner and even though we have auto-fault injection tests that run on the gate (for non-proxies) which in theory would catch regressions, changes like this are going to get additional human review of change itself.  We're also going to see if other places have this class of bug.  So sometime next week is our timeline.

https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/compare/mqtt-ws-proxy has wave 1 of the fix; it's not the final (there's false positive error messages and it may make sense to break this function up instead of the if checks).

    }

    IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIG client_config;

    IoTHubClient_SetConnectionStatusCallback(handle1, connection_status,

- **OS and version used:** Ubuntu 16.04.3 LTS

- **Protocol:** AMQP over Websockets

# Description of the issue:
After a successfull connection the network is disconnected and reconnected later. Depending on the timing the connection is not re-established again.

# Code sample exhibiting the issue:
(similar setup as in issue #251)
Take the `iothub_client/samples/iothub_client_sample_x509/iothub_client_sample_x509.c` and:

@davidbuechi , the frequency with which IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork is called depends on several factors, the top being how reliable a network is and how powerful the host device is.

Within the threaded layer of the Azure IoT C SDK (iothub_client.c), we call IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork every 1 millisecond. That in general is safe, but a little more frequent than most environments would require. Calling it once every second might be too slow for unreliable networks.

Starting on OS X El Capitan, Mac OS comes with SIP (System Integrity Protection) which blocks brew from installing/creating links over the existing paths on /usr/* (https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT204899)
After installing curl with brew and forcing link creations (into /usr/local/*), cmake is able to recognize the keg version of curl installed.
However since the original curl libraries are not overwritten (under /usr/lib), the application will still find the old libcurl.4.dylib (on High Sierra, 7.54.0) and use it, reproducing the bug described in this issue.
To complete the workaround one must set DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH.

# Description of the issue:
<!-- Please be as detailed as possible: which feature has a problem, how often does it fail,  -->
I'm working on a custom implementation of the MQTT sample, put in a state machine and set to push a single message in a user-selectable time interval (between 5 minutes and 1 hour). The requirements of the company I'm working for do not involve receiving C2D messages for now.

Having disabled a device in the IoT Hub and trying to connect to it for sending messages, the result is the client being stuck in an "idle" state after reaching the retry policy timeout (1 minute on IOTHUB_CLIENT_RETRY_EXPONENTIAL_BACKOFF_WITH_JITTER).

# Code sample exhibiting the issue:
<!-- Please remove any connection string information! -->
**Setup:**
_iothub_client_sample_mqtt_ modified in these points:
- Added Connection Status callback: it basically quits the main do-while loop after _CONN_RETRY_NUM_ (set to 4) unsuccessful connection attempts.
```
static void ConnStatCallback(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_STATUS result, IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_STATUS_REASON reason, void* userContextCallback)
{
    int* counter = (int*)userContextCallback;

    if (result == IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_AUTHENTICATED)
    {
        IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Attempt %d of %d: MQTT connection established", *counter, CONN_RETRY_NUM);
    }
    else
    {
        (*counter)++;

        if (reason == IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_BAD_CREDENTIAL)
        {
            IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Attempt %d of %d: Invalid Device Id or Shared Access Key", *counter, CONN_RETRY_NUM);
        }
        else if (reason == IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_COMMUNICATION_ERROR)
        {
            IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Attempt %d of %d: Communication error", *counter, CONN_RETRY_NUM);
        }
        else if (reason == IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_DEVICE_DISABLED)
        {
            IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Attempt %d of %d: Device disabled by IoT Hub", *counter, CONN_RETRY_NUM);
        }
        else if (reason == IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONNECTION_EXPIRED_SAS_TOKEN)
        {
            IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Attempt %d of %d: SAS Token expired", *counter, CONN_RETRY_NUM);
        }
    }

    IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("ConnStat callback counter = %d", *counter);
    if (*counter >= CONN_RETRY_NUM)
    {
        IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Maximum number of attempts reached, exiting IoT Hub Client");
        g_continueRunning = false;
    }
}
```

- Modified Send Confirmation callback, so as to quit the loop after one message:
```
static void SendConfirmationCallback(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_RESULT result, void* userContextCallback)
{
    EVENT_INSTANCE* eventInstance = (EVENT_INSTANCE*)userContextCallback;
    IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("Confirmation[%d] received for message tracking id = %zu with result = %s",
                    callbackCounter, eventInstance->messageTrackingId,
                    ENUM_TO_STRING(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_RESULT, result));

    callbackCounter++;
    IoTHubMessage_Destroy(eventInstance->messageHandle);

    // Quit after receiving last callback
    IOTHUB_LOGDEBUG("callbackCounter = %d", (int)callbackCounter);
    if (callbackCounter >= MESSAGE_COUNT)
    {
        g_continueRunning = false;
    }
}
```

title: Bob_UploadFromSasUri Timeout Value
body:
- **OS and version used:** Windows 7 x64
- **SDK version used:** Latest SDK

# Description of the issue:
Cannot find way to set timeout value.  Need way to recognize network connectivity loss and return from HTTPAPIEX_ExecuteRequet.

The Bob_UploadFromSasUri method from blob.c is being used to upload files to blob storage.  The default timeout is very long and a way to set the timeout to a lower value in order to response to loss of network connectivity in a timely manner is needed.  Unsuccessfully tried using the HTTPAPIEX_SetOption method using the OPTION_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT, OPTION_C2D_KEEP_ALIVE_FREQ_SECS, and OPTION_CBS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT options.

title: iothub_client_ll.h: some definitions are not wrapped in extern C
body:
Some definitions (e.g. `DEFINE_ENUM(IOTHUB_CLIENT_RESULT, IOTHUB_CLIENT_RESULT_VALUES);`) are not wrapped in `extern "C"` leading to linker errors when included in C++ code. Workaround is to wrap all includes in a top-level `extern "C"` block.

Release: 2018-03-02.
comments:
[2018-03-13T05:03:03Z | jspaith | comment]
Uhm, yes.  Thanks for letting us know about this.  We need to fix the header in SDK itself of course.

Could you help me understand your scenario here for this & #411?  Are you building IoT SDK as Windows DLL (or your code is a DLL and statically linking to Azure IoT SDK) and your app is C++?

[2018-03-13T06:21:42Z | zvrba | comment]
I'm building the SDK as static libs, as that's the default and there are fewer files to deploy. This particular app is a C++ Windows service that is also a COM component/server. (It links dynamically to the CRT). Other components in my SW package use the C# SDK which has been less.. bumpy :)

Re #411: I took the time to understand the enum macros and realized that these also define conversions to/from textual strings. When logging errors, I'd much more prefer to output a readable enum name than an int constant. So I hit #411.

More background: I'm building software for a product that is headless embedded device. I need to have strict control of all code that's going to run on the device and how it's built. [1] Therefore I build all native dependencies myself, install them under own directory (e.g. `C:\deps`) and put that directory into subversion. That way I get reproducible builds and can easily track what SW version each device is running (I'm also embedding VERSIONINFO including SVN revision in my executables/DLLs).

[1] I have also forsaken the "Debug" mode as it's ABI-incompatible with Release. I build all dependencies as Release, whereas the "Debug" configuration of my projects (I named it "RelNoOpt") is actually Release with all optimizations turned off so the debugging experience is still comfortable.

That's also the reason I'm not using vcpkg or NuGet prebuilt packages.

[2018-03-13T15:13:37Z | ras0219-msft | comment]
@zvrba As an aside, we definitely support that in Vcpkg by just setting the MSBuild property `VcpkgConfiguration` to `Release` in your project under your "RelNoOpt" configuration.

We can also make a nice, standalone folder for you to check into SVN via `vcpkg export --raw <packages>`!

[2018-03-13T15:18:38Z | zvrba | comment]
Oh, thanks for the vcpkg export tip. Didn't know it could do that!

Hi @lmussier,

The way I was able to repro this is by having the open (WebSockets connect) timeout when using WebSockets. Is that the way you observed it too?

There are 2 issues:

1.
The issue that you pointed out where I agree that we don't need to close if we're signaled via open_complete of an error or cancelled.

I'll check in your fix as soon as I can and let you know.

-----

2.
There is another issue that the open_complete with CANCELLED is indicated without setting the state to NOT_OPEN. This means that if the consumer calls close in the open_complete callback then the cycle would repeat.

After fixing this, I believe there is a deeper problem here.
wsio triggers callback from the underlying lws callback received from lws. This is an issue because the consumer of wsio could call close which would destroy the lws context, which would result in a crash.

As a note, in parallel we have an effort to replace lws with a more lightweight client only WebSocket implementation that would use our IO abstraction. This work is already started and I wonder if the above workaround that you proposed is good enough for you until we have the lws dependency replaced with the new uws_client we are putting in.

I think fixing this callback issue involves rewriting a lot of the wsio code, but that would already be obsolete by the time we put in the new wsio based on uws_client. Thus I would not make this fix now.

Thanks,
/Dan

             (void)strncpy(dst, src, srcLength);
                   ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    armv7at2hf-neon-fslc-linux-gnueabi/azure-c-shared-utility/1.1.4-r0/git/src/crt_abstractions.c:132:28: note: length computed here
         size_t srcLength = strlen(src);
                            ^~~~~~~~~~~
    armv7at2hf-neon-fslc-linux-gnueabi/azure-c-shared-utility/1.1.4-r0/git/src/crt_abstractions.c:149:23: error: 'strncpy' specified bound depends on the length of the source argument [-Werror=stringop-overflow=]
                 (void)strncpy(dst, src, srcLength);
                       ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    armv7at2hf-neon-fslc-linux-gnueabi/azure-c-shared-utility/1.1.4-r0/git/src/crt_abstractions.c:132:28: note: length computed here

title: Mqtt not timing out messages when can't reconnect
body:
Initially opened on https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-python/issues/216

If MQTT is unable to establish a connection, it will keep trying and once it succeeds queued messages will be sent to the Cloud.

However, if for some reason we can't get past the initial connection phase, then SDK does not respect message timeouts.  An easy way to repro this is to just send a few messages with networking enabled via convenience sample, then disable your network in middle.

What is happening is that in `IoTHubTransport_MQTT_Common_DoWork`, we have logic that will compare max # of retries and ultimately call `sendMsgComplete(mqttMsgEntry->iotHubMessageEntry, transport_data, IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT);` which tells caller that we should timeout.

However - if the initial call to `InitializeConnection` at the top of this function fails, then we never get into the correct spot in the loop to check the timeouts.  

Note there is at IoTHub_Client layer a `DoTimeouts` API.  However it doesn't save us here because its already transferred the messages from its pending queue to MQTT's waitingForAck.

To fix this
A) Checking for message timeouts should not be conditional on state of MQTT itself.  And 
B) It feels more natural to be the timeout based on actual timing, instead of checking whether a retry has occurred or not.  
C) The code in the block `Codes_SRS_IOTHUB_TRANSPORT_MQTT_COMMON_07_057` also needs review.  After we timeout the 1st timed out message, it looks like we unconditionally run through the queued messages and reset their retryCount=0.  If we just did (B) though, this would be moot.
symptom: Message delivery issues, Disconnetion issues, Reconnection issues

# Description of the issue:
I was having some issues with a race condition in my application shutdown when a device method callback was in progress. In an attempt to fix this, I added the following to the start of my shutdown function:
```
IoTHubDeviceClient_SetDeviceMethodCallback(iotHubClientHandle, NULL, NULL);
```
In the belief that this would unsubscribe me from callbacks. This seemed to execute successfully on my workstation but failed with the following error on ARM:
```
Error: Time:Tue Nov 20 18:51:10 2018 File:/usr/src/debug/azure-iot-sdk-c/1.2.10-r0/git/iothub_client/src/iothubtransportamqp_methods.c Func:iothubtransportamqp_methods_unsubscribe Line:897 unsubscribe called while not subscribed
```
The root cause seems to be that in IoTHubClientCore_LL_SetDeviceMethodCallback the subscribe function call uses the deviceHandle and the unsubscribe function call uses the transportHandle. 
The reason this seems to work against x86 and not on ARM appears to be in IoTHubTransport_AMQP_Common_Unsubscribe_DeviceMethod, when the value of device_state->subscribe_methods_needed is uninitialized on ARM it was 240 and on x86 it was 0. Since there is no else statement it just quietly fails.

Hi @ling0015, to try to understand your issue better I reproduced the error by creating a simple application that called `SetDeviceMethodCallBack` to subscribe then immediately called it again passing in NULL to unsubscribe from Device Methods. This was run on Visual Studio in Windows.

    (void)IoTHubDeviceClient_SetDeviceMethodCallback(device_handle, device_method_callback, NULL);

The information you provided on the error doesn't give us enough to understand exactly what issue you are running into. It could be that you are unsubscribing from the same connection twice, unsubscribing.

[2019-01-04T14:57:53Z | ling0015 | comment]
Hi @YoDaMa,
To clarify, I am not currently experiencing an issue with unsubscribing. My original issue was my application was destroying resources that were being used in callbacks, I originally attempted to use unsubscribe to address this issue. In the end I was able to use IoTHubClient_Destroy to wait for callbacks to close before destroying the resources to fix my problem. 

I opened this issue as it seemed like a bug you guys might be interested in. 

I believe you may be correct about the race condition because in the sample program attached the error is exhibited when the sleep on line 60 is small, and is not exhibited when it is large.

[main.txt](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/files/2727378/main.txt)

[2019-01-07T20:34:15Z | YoDaMa | comment]
Good to hear you managed the problem! As to your question, let me give it a crack. 

The difference between the two comes down to the fact that in particular with the AMQP protocol you have the option to use multiplexing through the transport to weave the data of multiple so-called 'Devices' through a single communication point. So a device handle will point to a struct that has information related to a 'Device'. A transport handle will point to a struct that has information related to the transport (AMQP).

To your question of why would subscribe use the device handle and unsubscribe use the transport handle, the question must be understood through the context of *where* the calls are being made. 

In `IoTHubClientCore_LL_SetDeviceMethodCallback` both calls for subscribe and unsubscribe are made using the device handle. This makes sense since we are calling into `IoTHubTransport_Subscribe`, which in AMQP takes in a device handle to subscribe that device to method callbacks (it doesn't make sense if you are multiplexing to use a transport handle to subscribe a single device to a method callback). 

In `iothubtransportamqp_methods_subscribe` we are just adjusting the device state to indicate that it needs to subscribe to methods. During the transport's DoWork call, it will check for this device state and if indicated it will update the transport by calling into `_iothubtransportamqp_methods_unsubscribe` which will unsubscribe the device via the transport method handle. 

Hopefully this explanation is helpful! If I didn't explain it well enough or answer your question don't be shy.

@larsonmpdx you hit a quirk with the gcc compiler, I'll try to explain (very poorly) below.  Moving the umqtt lib above aziotsharedutil will fix the issue and we shall fix our documentation to make it more clear.  Your target_link_libraries code should look like this:

target_link_libraries(myproject
        iothub_client
        iothub_client_mqtt_transport
        umqtt
        uhttp
        aziotsharedutil
        pthread
        curl
        ssl
        crypto

	  # prov_auth_client # causes conflicts on source-built sdk, nov 2018
	  # hsm_security_client # causes conflicts on source-built sdk, nov 2018
        uuid
        parson
        )

The reason this error occurred is that gcc gathers the dependencies as it goes along from top to bottom if a dependency is encountered of a library that has been previously scanned, the code won't be found, generating a undefined reference error.  The StringToken_Split is a new function and this is the first release where it's been used and it's only being used in umqtt.  Since no other library above the aziotsharedutil is using that function when gcc get to that library it discards that function to save space, not knowing that later on umqtt will need this function.

body:
- **OS and version used:** Linux

- **SDK version used:** release_2018_10_03

# Description of the issue:
The problem to be solved is that the attempt to connect to Azure sometimes fails at the low level, and the low level debug messages make this plain, but nothing is communicated back to the high level functions that we are using. (Either they return void, or the cases where they return an opaque handle only fail when something seriously bad happens, like a malloc failure or null input argument.) Examples would be an unauthorized ConnectionString or bad proxy settings. Without this, much time passes until you find that you can’t send messages; that is your clue that the connection was not opened.

The callback for the Connection Status change is not being invoked here, presumably because it has not yet *changed*.

Looking at the existing Azure APIs, none is quite right for getting at this. Adding a getter for the Connection Status would be one option, though that may be a fair amount of work since the mocking function must also be provided, and tests to validate it.

What I chose to do was to patch the closest of the existing APIs, GetSendStatus. Normally this returns IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK if it is able to get the SendStatus (which is either Idle or Busy, returned as an output parameter). My simple patch was to return IOTHUB_CLIENT_ERROR from the low level IoTHubTransport_AMQP_Common_GetSendStatus() function if transport’s state is not Connected or Connecting.

I think a better choice, if still using the same API signature for GetSendStatus, would be to extend the set of enums from just Idle and Busy to add NotConnected or somesuch. The justification for leaning on this API could be that NotConnected is an indication of "why you can’t Send right now".

# Code sample exhibiting the issue:
My patch, for AMQP over websockets, is provided here. I recommend adding the new enum instead of what I did, but the patch shows the way. I think MQTT will have a similar solution.
[ll_ampq_extensions.patch.txt](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/files/2634678/ll_ampq_extensions.patch.txt)

# Description of the issue:

title: Desired twin updates gets reverted when a connection is restored
body:
- Windows 10.0.17763.194
- Azure C-SDK 1.2.10

# Description of the issue:
I’m seeing a very weird issue – basically, I do the following:
 
- Client gets connected and receives the full device twin as expected.
- Iunplug the network cable of the device. 
   - The client SDK output shows that it lost connectivity and is retrying. The pause between each try increases as expected.
- I update the device twin desired properties using Device Explorer. 
    - Hitting refresh shows the new values as expected.
- I plug-in the network cable again. 
    - The client SDK output shows that it regained connectivity.
    - I wait a few seconds, and it successfully gets the entire device twin again.
 
Now, at this point, I expect to get the updates I made in #3 – however, I get the old version. Moreover, if I look at the desired properties using Device Explorer, I see my changes from #3 got reverted. The version stamp remains the same – but the values are the old one.

typedef struct MESSAGE_INSTANCE_TAG
{
	IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE messageHandle;
	size_t messageTrackingId;  // For tracking the messages within the user callback.
}
MESSAGE_INSTANCE;

size_t messagesReceivedByInput1Queue = 0;

// SendConfirmationCallback is invoked when the message that was forwarded on from 'InputQueue1Callback'
// pipeline function is confirmed.
static void SendConfirmationCallback(IOTHUB_CLIENT_CONFIRMATION_RESULT result, void* userContextCallback)
{
	// The context corresponds to which message# we were at when we sent.
	MESSAGE_INSTANCE* messageInstance = (MESSAGE_INSTANCE*)userContextCallback;
	printf("Confirmation[%zu] received for message with result = %d\r\n", messageInstance->messageTrackingId, result);
	IoTHubMessage_Destroy(messageInstance->messageHandle);
	free(messageInstance);
}

// Allocates a context for callback and clones the message
// NOTE: The message MUST be cloned at this stage.  InputQueue1Callback's caller always frees the message
// so we need to pass down a new copy.
static MESSAGE_INSTANCE* CreateMessageInstance(IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE message)
{
	MESSAGE_INSTANCE* messageInstance = (MESSAGE_INSTANCE*)malloc(sizeof(MESSAGE_INSTANCE));
	if (NULL == messageInstance)
	{
		printf("Failed allocating 'MESSAGE_INSTANCE' for pipelined message\r\n");
	}
	else
	{
		memset(messageInstance, 0, sizeof(*messageInstance));

		if ((messageInstance->messageHandle = IoTHubMessage_Clone(message)) == NULL)
		{
			free(messageInstance);
			messageInstance = NULL;
		}
		else
		{
			messageInstance->messageTrackingId = messagesReceivedByInput1Queue;
		}
	}

	return messageInstance;
}

static IOTHUBMESSAGE_DISPOSITION_RESULT InputQueue1Callback(IOTHUB_MESSAGE_HANDLE message, void* userContextCallback)
{
	IOTHUBMESSAGE_DISPOSITION_RESULT result;
	IOTHUB_CLIENT_RESULT clientResult;
	IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE iotHubModuleClientHandle = (IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE)userContextCallback;

	unsigned const char* messageBody;
	size_t contentSize;

	if (IoTHubMessage_GetByteArray(message, &messageBody, &contentSize) != IOTHUB_MESSAGE_OK)
	{
		messageBody = NULL;
	}

	printf("Received Message [%zu]\r\n Data: [%s]\r\n",
		messagesReceivedByInput1Queue, messageBody);

	// This message should be sent to next stop in the pipeline, namely "output1".  What happens at "outpu1" is determined
	// by the configuration of the Edge routing table setup.
	MESSAGE_INSTANCE *messageInstance = CreateMessageInstance(message);
	if (NULL == messageInstance)
	{
		result = IOTHUBMESSAGE_ABANDONED;
	}
	else
	{
		printf("Sending message (%zu) to the next stage in pipeline\n", messagesReceivedByInput1Queue);

		clientResult = IoTHubModuleClient_LL_SendEventToOutputAsync(iotHubModuleClientHandle, messageInstance->messageHandle, "output1", SendConfirmationCallback, (void *)messageInstance);
		if (clientResult != IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK)
		{
			IoTHubMessage_Destroy(messageInstance->messageHandle);
			free(messageInstance);
			printf("IoTHubModuleClient_LL_SendEventToOutputAsync failed on sending msg#=%zu, err=%d\n", messagesReceivedByInput1Queue, clientResult);
			result = IOTHUBMESSAGE_ABANDONED;
		}
		else
		{
			result = IOTHUBMESSAGE_ACCEPTED;
		}
	}

	messagesReceivedByInput1Queue++;
	return result;
}

static IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE InitializeConnection()
{
	IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE iotHubModuleClientHandle;

	if (IoTHub_Init() != 0)
	{
		printf("Failed to initialize the platform.\r\n");
		iotHubModuleClientHandle = NULL;
	}
	else if ((iotHubModuleClientHandle = IoTHubModuleClient_LL_CreateFromEnvironment(MQTT_Protocol)) == NULL)
	{
		printf("ERROR: IoTHubModuleClient_LL_CreateFromEnvironment failed\r\n");
	}
	else

		// IoTHubModuleClient_LL_SetOption(iotHubModuleClientHandle, OPTION_LOG_TRACE, &trace);
	}

	return iotHubModuleClientHandle;
}

static void DeInitializeConnection(IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE iotHubModuleClientHandle)
{
	if (iotHubModuleClientHandle != NULL)
	{
		IoTHubModuleClient_LL_Destroy(iotHubModuleClientHandle);
	}
	IoTHub_Deinit();
}

static int SetupCallbacksForModule(IOTHUB_MODULE_CLIENT_LL_HANDLE iotHubModuleClientHandle)
{
	int ret;

	if (IoTHubModuleClient_LL_SetInputMessageCallback(iotHubModuleClientHandle, "input1", InputQueue1Callback, (void*)iotHubModuleClientHandle) != IOTHUB_CLIENT_OK)
	{
		printf("ERROR: IoTHubModuleClient_LL_SetInputMessageCallback(\"input1\")..........FAILED!\r\n");
		ret = __FAILURE__;
	}

	{
		ret = 0;
	}

}

void iothub_module()
{

	srand((unsigned int)time(NULL));

	if ((iotHubModuleClientHandle = InitializeConnection()) != NULL && SetupCallbacksForModule(iotHubModuleClientHandle) == 0)

title: concurency issue with blob upload
body:
- **OS and version used:** Ubuntu 18.04

- **SDK version used:** lts_10_2018

# Description of the issue:
Hi,

From the [iothubclient_requirements](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/blob/master/iothub_client/devdoc/requirement_docs/iothubclient_requirements.md#overview), the high-level API should be thread-safe (unlike the low-level one). However, the blob upload interface does not respect this. 

When the `IoTHubClientCore_UploadToBlobAsync` function is called, a dedicated thread is spawned. the low-level function `IoTHubClientCore_LL_UploadToBlob` is then called within this thread, triggering the process of blob upload. 

If the function `IoTHubClientCore_UploadToBlobAsync` is called multiple times, nothing prevent threads to be launched. On Linux platform using curl adapter, `HTTPAPI_Init` function will be called multiple times. This may result in a concurrent access of the `nUsersOfHTTPAPI` variable, thus interfering with the calls to `curl_global_init` and `curl_global_cleanup`.

How can we prevent this? Is allowing only one blob upload at a time the correct behavior?

Regards,
Alexis.

Clone the PAL Repo (you need recursive because the C SDK is included as a submodule):

Navigate to the build_all directory:

Run make_sdk.cmd, specifying the location of the Arduino Library on your machine:

I had the same issues and finally got a working setup by installing certain specific versions. Others pointed out that they got it working by rollback to an older version, but I could not find a working set of compatible versions anywhere. Please always mention the specific version as this may help others reading your messages! 
I hope it helps others when I explain what I did. 

At first, installing different version of the esp8266 board and the AzureIoT libraries did not help me. I was getting the same "sort of" compile errors. So then I decided to remove all the installed versions from disk. First close Arduino IDE, and then remove the folders (paths for MacOS):
- `~/Library/Arduino15/packages` (the board) 
- `~/Documents/Arduino/libraries` (the libraries)

Finally install the exactly the following versions.
Board: 
 - esp8266 (by ESP8266 community) - 2.4.2

Libraries:
 - Azureiothub - 1.0.45
 - Azureiotprotocol_mqtt - 1.0.45
 - azureiotutility - 1.0.45

I don't think the problems would relate to a specific version of the Arduino IDE, but to make it complete, this was all done in Arduino IDE v1.8.10. 

To prove that the complete solution worked I used this guide to read data from Azure IoT hub which was sent by the ESP8266: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/iot-hub/quickstart-send-telemetry-node#code-try-2

`

You have GatewayHostname, but the correct value is GatewayHostName – note the capital ‘N’ in name.  This is why the argument is ignored and you’re always hitting the hub.

In the perfect world I’d make the client just fail if it doesn’t recognize a value, but thanks to back-compat I’m afraid to do that. I think what we should do though is LogError() when we don’t recognize output (along with a note that the error is going to be ignored and we'll keep on parsing).

- **OS and version used:** FreeRTOS

- **SDK version used:** 1.2.13


# Description of the issue:
Dear All,

I’m writing this issue about some difficulties in the managing of X.509 certificate and of private key in my IoT device.

I use the 1.2.13 release version of C Device SDK in my embedded platform and I choose the MQTT protocol for the communication between my IoT device and IoT Hub. The MQTT is made secure through the TLS layer implemented by the mbedTLS library.

In the first part of my test I use a Sas authentication device and all works fine. I set only one client option, _OPTION_TRUSTED_CERT_, in way to guarantee a successfully one way TLS authentication.

In the second part of my test I use a self signed authentication device. So I set three client options:  _OPTION_TRUSTED_CERT_, _SU_OPTION_X509_CERT_ and _SU_OPTION_X509_PRIVATE_KEY_. However my device, during the TLS handshake, provides a null certificate, then the IoT Hub can’t authenticate my device.
The client options are configured successfully through the _IoTHubClient_LL_SetOption_ function. 
In order to run my MQTT client I invoke the _IoTHubClient_LL_DoWork_ function.
Before the establishment of the MQTT connection between my IoT device and IoT Hub I notice that the client options are resetted inside the _ResetConnectionIfNecessary_ function. Theoretically all the existing client options are first retrieved and then saved before the cancellation through the _xio_retrieveoptions_ and _set_saved_tls_options_ functions respectively. However the _xio_retrieveoptions_->_tlsio_mbedtls_retrieveoptions_ function don’t retrieved the _SU_OPTION_X509_CERT_ and _SU_OPTION_X509_PRIVATE_KEY_ client options, so they aren’t saved.
Before the MQTT connection, the client options previously saved are restored through the _GetTransportProviderIfNecessary_->_OptionHandler_FeedOptions_ function. Unfortunately the _SU_OPTION_X509_CERT_ and _SU_OPTION_X509_PRIVATE_KEY_ client options isn’t saved and so they can’t be restored.
For this reason during the TLS handshake my IoT device provides a null certificate and this invalidates the authentication procedure in IoT Hub.

At this point I would ask how can I fix this problem? Should I implement custom code inside the _tlsio_mbedtls_retrieveoptions_ function in order to retrieve the _SU_OPTION_X509_CERT_ and _SU_OPTION_X509_PRIVATE_KEY_ client options? Or is there some other function already ready?.

Thanks in advance.
Regards.
Matteo

title: Version 1.2.14 Memory Leak when client handle is released while MQTT trying to reconnect
comments:
[2019-03-25T18:07:41Z | ewertons | comment]
Hi @maskimthedog ,
thanks for reporting this issue! Sorry for the memory leak, that is a high-priority issue and we will address right away.

[2019-04-01T18:42:27Z | jebrando | comment]
@maskimthedog,

I'm looking into this bug and have one question.  Do you the exact steps to repro this issue.

Thanks,
Jelani

[2019-04-01T18:48:00Z | maskimthedog | comment]
Attempting to close the client handle while MQTT over websockets is continuously trying to reconnect on failed MQTT ping.

[2019-04-01T18:51:09Z | maskimthedog | comment]
I am using the LL calls on a single thread.

[2019-04-01T18:51:54Z | maskimthedog | comment]
I can send you my code if need be.

[2019-04-16T19:31:23Z | maskimthedog | comment]
I believe what is happening is this...

MQTT connection is active and a ping failure occurs because of a signal disruption.
Then transport_data->currPacketState != DISCONNECT_TYPE when DisconnectFromClient() is called the transport is freed and transport_data->currPacketState is set to DISCONNECT_TYPE within the function.
Next the SDK attempts to reconnect calling InitializeConnection() which calls ResetConnectionIfNecessary() freeing up the transport (if a connection attempt has been made previously) prior to calling SendMqttConnectMsg() which calls GetTransportProviderIfNecessary() to allocate the transport.
This all plays well until IoTHubTransport_MQTT_Common_Destroy() is called which calls DisconnectFromClient().  Since transport_data->currPacketState is still set to DISCONNECT_TYPE, DisconnectFromClient() does not free the transport.

[2019-04-24T11:37:18Z | maskimthedog | comment]
Ping.

[2019-08-17T23:56:56Z | maskimthedog | comment]
This bug still exists in 1.3.4.  The fix is still the same.

[2019-08-27T04:33:20Z | rafilho | comment]
Thanks for reporting it, @maskimthedog, and sorry for the long time with no activity. We will look into it. Thanks.

[2019-08-28T19:21:35Z | jspaith | comment]
@maskimthedog - agree with your analysis of this.  I think a safer fix here though is to add in `free_transport_handle_data` logic the `xio_destroy(transport_data->xioTransport)` call.   

`free_transport_handle_data` acts as the "destructor" of the handle.  So by putting the `xio_destroy` call here we make sure that any code path - now or future - does not have to rely on `DisconnectFromClient` being in just the right state first.  

Also the `if (transport_data->currPacketState != DISCONNECT_TYPE)` in disconnect does provide a useful service of making sure we don't send multiple disconnect packets to server.  So I'd rather leave that alone.

I've reviewed code and don't see other such leaks.  For something of this severity though I'll need further consultation with my colleagues.  If you have any concerns with my fix please let me know as you've obviously gone quite deep into this code.

Thanks for your excellent analysis on this and to echo @rafilho apologies on delays here.

[2019-08-29T18:14:12Z | maskimthedog | comment]
No worries.  Thanks for the patch.  I am testing now with it applied to 1.3.4.
