backend_1     |   devEUI: '02000000efbeadde',
backend_1     |   reference: '',
backend_1     |   acknowledged: false,
backend_1     |   fCnt: 43 }
````

This occurs even with disabled frame count validation turned on.

### What version are your using?
0.21.1 (R-Pi APT Repo)

### How can your issue be reproduced?
This python3 script with aiohttp package can reproduce:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Reproduces duplicate fCnt when queuing packets for downlink
# This script causes NUM_PACKETS of many async requests to the queue API endpoint
# Requires python3, asyncio and aiohttp module

import aiohttp
import asyncio
import base64

NUM_PACKETS=10
url = 'https://localhost:8080/api'
username = 'admin'
password = 'admin'
deveui = '02000000efbeadde'

def b64encode(payload):
    return base64.b64encode(bytes(payload)).decode('utf-8')

async def queue_packet(payload, headers):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(connector=aiohttp.TCPConnector(verify_ssl=False)) as session:
        async with session.post('%s/devices/%s/queue' % (url, deveui),
                                json={'data': b64encode(payload), 
                                      'confirmed': True}, headers=headers) as resp:
            print(await resp.json())

async def main():
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(connector=aiohttp.TCPConnector(verify_ssl=False)) as session:
        async with session.post('%s/internal/login' % url,
                                json={'username': username, 
                                      'password': password}) as resp:
            resp_json = await resp.json()
            print(resp_json)
            headers = {'authorization': resp_json['jwt'] }
            # Make some arbitrary data for the packet payload
            for x in range(NUM_PACKETS):
                payload = [y for y in range(0, x*NUM_PACKETS, x+1)]
                asyncio.ensure_future(queue_packet(payload, headers))
    # 10sec should be enough to make these requests
    await asyncio.sleep(10)

loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
loop.run_until_complete(main())

title: Possible issue with frame count reaching 65535
body:
Hi there

I have been running a test mote for a few days now and today I started getting the following error with devEUI:

> {"devEUI":"0000000079250001","type":"DATA_UP_MIC","error":"invalid MIC"}

The log entries are as follows:

> Oct 27 10:28:52 iotlab02 lora-app-server[15272]: time="2016-10-27T10:28:52+02:00" level=error msg="invalid MIC" dev_eui=0000000079250001 type=DATA_UP_MIC
> Oct 27 10:28:52 iotlab02 lora-app-server[15272]: time="2016-10-27T10:28:52+02:00" level=info msg="handler/mqtt: publishing error notification" topic="application/0000000000000000/node/0000000079250001/error"
> Oct 27 10:28:52 iotlab02 loraserver[15233]: time="2016-10-27T10:28:52+02:00" level=error msg="processing rx packet error: invalid MIC" data_base64="QAEAJXmAdg4BvV+qY82d0bcu7h9xMFhIAqm1iO3qCremu1DlZeztNWHaDsvqUCWZKg=="

The only thing I noticed is that on the Lora-app-server, the frame counter seemed to have stopped at 65535.

Restarting the mote resets the frame counter, and all transmissions resumed as normal.

Could the frame counter be overflowing, thereby causing the error. 

I'm using version **0.12.3** for the **loraserver** and **0.1.3** for the **apps** server.
comments: [2016-11-14T11:44:17Z | andrepferreira | comment] Quick update. I have been able to replicate this issue as my mote has once again reached 65535 packets and the same MIC error above has appeared. Below is the view of the frame count from the App-Server node config page. (keys removed for security) [2016-11-14T18:39:39Z | brocaar | comment] @andrepferreira I'm just back from vacation so I haven't had the change to look into it sooner. Anyway, I'm able to replicate it and will look into a fix asap. [2016-11-14T19:21:42Z | brocaar | comment] I've found the issue. I might have introduced this bug during splitting the lora app server logic out of loraserver. What happens is: The counter (32 bit) is incremented to 65536 at the side of the node (this value is used for the MIC) and because of this, the `FCnt` which is 16 bit is transmitted as 0, as it contains the 16 LSB. The server is able to detect the 16 bit rollover, but because the MIC validation is happening before the `FCnt` expansion, it is using the wrong `FCnt` to validate the MIC (so it is validated against 0 instead of 65536). I have a fix working locally and will add a testcase to make sure this regression won't be re-introduced again :-) [2016-11-14T19:47:44Z | brocaar | comment] See https://github.com/brocaar/loraserver/commit/2849d0298ce44153876b878183043b5a5f5b9747 for the fix. Once the build is green, it will be released as loraserver 0.12.4. Thanks for reporting this bug!

title: Strange neighbor solicit after reboot
body:
Setup is 6lbr on BBB with cc2531/cc2538 usb SLIP, and 1 x cc2650 sensortag with bleeding edge contiki running 6lbr client only.

I let 6lbr and node go to a steady-state and then reboot the 6lbr. After booting, I see:
1. 6lbr transmitting DIOs, source fe80::212:4b00:413:396a
2. Node transmit DAO with old DODAG
3. 6lbr transmit Neighbor Solicitation with IPv6 address: Source ::0000 and destination fe80::1:ff13:396a. (note, two last octet same as himself)
4. 6lbr repeat transmission 3 times with ~10 sec intervals
5. Normal operation

It seems this is triggered by the DAO from the node, maybe he gets confused of the DODAG matching himself? I observed and reproduced it on 1.3.x, 95% sure I saw it on master as well.

Capture from sniffer. 6lbr is :212:4b00:413:396a, node is :0709
http://filebin.ca/2D9ibfbeoMz1/6lbrBootOneCC2650withCetic6lbrClient.pcapng

Level 10 log during boot:
https://gist.github.com/arurke/b46bd108ddebffbe9c6f

Regards,
Andreas U.
www.netwurke.com

title: tap0 interface not being removed at watchdog failure
body:
Hi,
I spend too much time in an ifup script which cause the watchdog to fail. When the 6lbr resets, the tap0 interface is still present which causes 6lbr to go into an endless loop with "FATAL: TAP: tun_alloc() : Device or resource busy". Please see the log at level 10:
https://gist.github.com/arurke/e4387686daf7cb774dc0

I do nothing to tap0 in the ifup script except
ethtool --offload tap0 gso off
ethtool --offload tap0 gro off

My 6lbr.conf:
MODE=SMART-BRIDGE
RAW_ETH=0
BRIDGE=0
DEV_BRIDGE=br0
DEV_TAP=tap0
DEV_ETH=eth0
RAW_ETH_FCS=0
DEV_RADIO=/dev/ttyO1

Am I assuming correctly that it is the responsibility of 6lbr to remove this interface? I.e. I should not add handling for it in the ifdown scripts?
comments:
[2016-02-29T20:43:29Z | laurentderu | comment]
A dynamically created tap interface is destroyed automatically when the endpoint is closed. Also, the existence of tap0 should not be a problem, 6LBR can open an existing tap interface (which can be useful if you're using the tap interface elsewhere and don't want the tap id to change). However, if another process still has that interface locked, 6LBR can not claim it and so it fails.

So maybe ethtool somehow claim (or keep a lock on) the tap interface, or the watchdog script failed to kill the previous 6lbr process, but I don't think so as the log shows the correct shutdown log.

[2016-03-01T16:30:22Z | arurke | comment]
So you think this is specific for my setup, not a general issue? Afaik I do nothing with tap0 at all. The last line in my 60dev ifup script configures Jool to use it, but this line is never executed since the code before (infinite loop of trying to establish 3G modem connection) does not complete. In addition Jool is removed in the ifdown. I will try to replace the 3G code with a 120sec sleep to see if this can impact.

[2016-03-01T18:42:46Z | laurentderu | comment]
The tap interface created by 6LBR is by default transient, so it should disappear when it gets killed. That means something is keeping it open. Could you check if there are no remaining 6lbr processes running ?

If it has been made persistent by one of the ifup scripts, you can try to force the deletion of the interface by using either 'tunctl -d tap0' or 'ip link delete tap0'

[2016-03-05T14:55:13Z | arurke | comment]
I exchanged the 3G modem setup with a very long sleep (PS! the watchdog interval is a lot more than the stated 60 seconds, closer to 2-3 min). My 60dev ifup looks like this:

```
#!/bin/bash
. $CETIC_6LBR_CONF
. $1/6lbr-functions
config_default
MODE_6LBR=$2
DEV=$3
OS=`uname`
ip -6 address add fd51:542a:930e:0000::2/64 dev tap0
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding=1
sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
ethtool --offload tap0 gso off
ethtool --offload tap0 gro off
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
sleep 250`
```

I still see the same issue. Regarding your question on remaining processes, it might be this is the issue:

After watchdog timeout and in continuous restart of 6lbr:

```
admin@beaglebone:~$ ps -aux | grep 6lbr
root       465  0.1  0.4   2868  2104 ?        S    14:57   0:00 /bin/bash /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr /etc/6lbr/6lbr.conf
root       523  0.0  0.1   1444   864 ?        S    14:57   0:00 sh -c /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr-ifup tap tap0 2>&1
root       526  0.0  0.4   2848  2084 ?        S    14:57   0:00 /bin/bash /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr-ifup tap tap0
root       565  0.0  0.4   2852  2088 ?        S    14:57   0:00 /bin/bash /etc/6lbr/ifup.d/60dev /usr/lib/6lbr tap tap0
```

After a normal start of 6lbr:

```
admin@beaglebone:~$ ps -aux | grep 6lbr
root       457  0.0  0.4   2868  2088 ?        S    14:51   0:00 /bin/bash /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr /etc/6lbr/6lbr.conf
root       493  2.2  0.3   2164  1588 ?        S    14:51   0:05 /usr/lib/6lbr/bin/cetic_6lbr_smart_bridge -c /etc/6lbr/nvm.dat -s /dev/ttyO1 -t tap0 -R -B 460800 -U /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr-ifup -D /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr-ifdown -w /usr/lib/6lbr/www -L 10 -W /var/log/6lbr.timestamp -P 60 -C /var/log/6lbr.ip -m /usr/lib/6lbr/plugins
root       494  0.5  0.3   2868  1724 ?        S    14:51   0:01 /bin/bash /usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr /etc/6lbr/6lbr.conf

```

At first glance there is at least one extra process than in the normal startup. Was this what you were expecting?

Deleting the interface in ifdown will solve it, however:
Two side-notes: 
The ifdown script is called after the watchdog restart, but it is not called in the later continuous reboots:

```
2016-02-05 14:00:20.892753: FATAL: TAP: tun_alloc() : Device or resource busy
********************************************************************************
Sat Mar 5 14:00:21 UTC 2016 : Starting 6LBR
```

And the same happens when doing "service 6lbr restart": The log says it runs ifdown but I cannot see my echos from the actual script.

```
2016-02-05 14:29:58.293771: FATAL: TAP: signal 15
2016-02-05 14:29:58.297462: INFO: TAP: Running 6lbr-ifdown script '/usr/lib/6lbr/6lbr-ifdown'
********************************************************************************
Sat Mar 5 14:29:58 UTC 2016 : Starting 6LBR
```

[2017-03-13T17:06:26Z | arurke | comment]
I have moved away from this setup so I will not investigate it further. Also I believe this was a very special use-case, and no one else has reported anything similar - so I'll just close the issue.

I also had alignment traps on an arm. The memory access addresses in the trap messages showed the problem was in accessing the uip_buf buffer, more specificly in the UIP_IP_BUF part. I suspected it was an alignment problem of the UIP_IP_BUF uip_ip_hdr struct into the uip_buf array, tried increasing `UIP_CONF_LLH_LEN` to 16 and the alignment traps went away.

// IP packet must be 4 bytes aligned

It seems I still have something to fix though, but the alignment traps went away.

title: Fragmentation failure when packet throughput is high
body: When many packets that requires fragmentation are forwarded by 6LBR towards WSN, the fragmentation system fails and only the first fragment of every packet is sent until the traffic slows down.
comments:
[2013-09-02T19:58:36Z | laurentderu | comment]
The issue arises when the queuebuf is (almost) full. Packets are fragmented, but there are not enough buffer available for all the fragments and the last fragments are dropped. However the fragmentation code does not remove the already scheduled fragments. So, in the end, only the first fragment of all packets is sent.

Solution is to check if enough buffers are available for all the fragments before starting the fragmentation mechanism. (And also increases the amount of available buffers)

title: 6lbr can't ping neighbour, route via (null)
body:
I've got a 6lbr running on a beaglebone and a single device connected to it. I can see the status packet being sent from the node every minute when using a sniffer. The node is running web-demo with contiki @ a38cfc8 on a custom platform with a CC1310 radio. Initially it worked great, but after about 2 hours 6lbr can't talk to the node, even though it continually receives the node's packets.

I'm not 100% sure on my 6lbr version, unfortunately, but we installed with a cetic-6lbr_1.4.0_armhf.deb with MD5 284f6b385048acf4d7135107d0d95212  .

In the sensors list its status frequently changes from OK to NR, and its route is often removed. When it gets added, its state is typically:

> fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202/128 via (null) 7678 s

The device's last seen never really goes above 60 seconds, so the BR is receiving its pings. It's always in the neighbor list and marked as REACHABLE. However, if I try and ping the node, I get nothing back:

> root@beaglebone:~# ping6 -c 1 fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202
> PING fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202(fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202) 56 data bytes
> 
> --- fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202 ping statistics ---
> 1 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 0ms
> 

If I look at the sniffer, I don't see anything getting sent out. However, I do notice frequent ICMPv6 pings from the node to 6lbr, which get replies. Not sure what these are, but am guessing it's part of normal RPL traffic? I also see 6lbr's DIO broadcasts, so its radio is obviously working. 

Restarting the node doesn't fix it, and I haven't restarted 6lbr yet because I don't want to lose an opportunity to get some useful debugging done. Probably worth noting that web/coap also don't work when the ping doesn't. 

Traceroute shows that the packet gets sent to the radio, but that's about it.

> traceroute to fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202 (fd00::212:4b00:d2d:c202), 30 hops max, 80 byte packets
>  1  fd00::212:4b00:a27:c7e4 (fd00::212:4b00:a27:c7e4)  3.973 ms  3.964 ms  3.977 ms
>  2  * * *
>  ...
> 30  * * *
> 

Any suggestions for narrowing down the cause? I've attached my seemingly uninteresting 6lbr.log and a pcap if you're interested, (`d2d:c202` is the node, `a27:c7e4` is the slip radio). 

[6lbr.log.txt](https://github.com/cetic/6lbr/files/829805/6lbr.log.txt)
[single-node-6lbr-cant-talk-to-node.zip](https://github.com/cetic/6lbr/files/829806/single-node-6lbr-cant-talk-to-node.zip)
comments:
[2017-03-09T09:09:53Z | laurentderu | comment]
The problem is that, for unknown reason, the neighbor entry for your node has been removed from the neighbor table of 6LBR, this is the (null) in the routing table. Because of that, the BR is no longer able to forward the packets towards your node as the next hop of the configured route does not exist anymore.

Now the root cause is not clear to me at all, and as you said, the 6lbr.log file does not show anything useful. To be able to analyse further, you should enable the traces in uip-ds6-nbr and maybe also in uip-ds6-route, rpl-dag and rpl-icmp6.
Note that 6LBR 1.4.x is still based on Contiki 3.0, on the other hand, 6LBR 1.5.x, the current develop branch, is based on the latest version of Contiki which contains updates and fixes related to the neighbor table management. It quite possible that you are observing a bug that is already solved, so before digging too much into the issue I would suggest to try with the latest version of the develop branch.

Btw, the ping you observe is in fact not related to RPL, it's a feature of the cc26xx-web-demo firmware which ping periodically its parent to get the current RSSI.

[2017-03-09T23:41:56Z | unknown_author | comment]
I'll test the develop branch and see if the issue remains. Just tried it now and the webserver fails after responding to one query, so need to figure out what's going on there. 

Will let you know how it goes.

[2017-03-13T03:14:36Z | unknown_author | comment]
So I've looked into this a bit today and saw it kind of happen again. This is against commit 744ad0cd1c0ee75136e09b11e8e7160208418683.

Soon after building the code, but before adding any debugging, I had the node connect, reliably ping 6lbr and be marked as NR. I couldn't tell why it had no route, but saw that it happened. It wasn't listed as `via (null)`, it just wasn't there. 

**edit:** Just noticed it again. I believe this happens if a) node is connected to 6lbr, b) 6lbr is restarted, c) node doesn't realize it's been restarted so thinks it's on the same dag.

I then enabled printing in `uip-ds6-nbr.c`, `uip-ds6-route.c`, `rpl-icmp6.c` and `rpl.c` and tried to make it happen again. I couldn't get it to happen by itself, but if I removed the route via the web interface it'd remain as NR for about an hour, at which point I reset it. When the node rejoined it was given a route, so that obviously isn't the issue I noted before.

Anyway, looked through the code and saw that a route is only ever added when a node sends a DAO, which happens when it changes dag/parent. So if a route is removed for whatever reason, the node remains unreachable for quite a period of time, and as far as I can tell, it will have no idea. 

So... should a route be added when we receive data from a node? Or maybe a DAO requested? I'm not terribly familiar with RPL, so maybe this is a dumb suggestion, but it seems weird to be able to receive from a node for so long without giving it a route, and without it knowing it doesn't have a route.

I'm going to reset the test and leave it running overnight to see if I can get the other issue to happen again.

[2017-03-15T09:09:55Z | laurentderu | comment]
In a RPL network, a downward route is only created when a valid DAO message is received. If a data packet is received from a node, a route is not created, otherwise you could have several downward routes towards the same node, some of them even not working as the radio conditions have changed.

In Contiki, the route created by RPL are protected, meaning that a route (and the corresponding next hop) will only be removed when an explicit No Path DAO (remove route message) or if the route lifetime has expired, or if there is a global or local repair.

In your case, the next hop has been deleted without removing the route, so it's most certainly a bug in the Contiki stack.

If you remove a route via the web interface, the end node does not know its route has been deleted so no new route will be created until the previous route lifetime is expired. To force recreation of the route you must trigger a global repair on the RPL page.

[2017-11-09T15:00:38Z | laurentderu | comment]
This was solved in cfbc964d6d843774c71ee3539a5ce11a68350fa9

title: First packet towards an Ethernet new neighbour contains RPL HBH extension header
body: The first packet towards an Ethernet new neighbour (the packet that has triggered a NS/NA handshake) contains RPL Hop-by-Hop extension header. Because of that extension header, the packet is dropped by the host. This explains why sometimes the connexion towards 6LBR seems to hang but is fine when we refresh the page.

title: Neighbor cache can only hold one IP per link local address
body:
Hello,
I could not manage to set up 6lbr in SMART_BRIDGE mode (develop branch) on a Raspberry Pi to reach IP addresses NDP_Proxied IPs from docker containers on a host in my network.

This led me to take a look at the source and I was surprised to see, that the IPv6 neighbor cache implemented in `core/net/ipv6/uip-ds6-nbr.c` is uniquely indexed on the link local address.
In my understanding it should be very well possible to have multiple IP entries for the same link local address in an IPv6 neighbor cache. Or am I mistaken? In fact, `ip -6 neigh` yields lots of duplicate lladdrs for me and seems to be just fine with it.

This limitation already becomes a problem when you have hosts with Privacy Extensions enabled on your network, since they will configure two IP addresses but only one of them can ever be stored by 6lbr at the same time - an issue I have also encountered already when trying to reach my dev machine from 6LoWPAN.

Could you tell me if you think this is a bug and if there is a mode/configuration where this would not be an issue? Thanks!
comments:
[2017-06-14T13:31:13Z | laurentderu | comment]
The limitation of one IP address per MAC address is indeed a limitation of the current neighbor table implementation of Contiki, even having both a link local and a global address should not be possible, but there is a loophole allowing this. This is an oversimplification that is perfectly fine for RPL network, but breaks when using more vanilla IPv6 configuration.

There is a workaround implemented in 6LBR, but it's rather limited. There is also a PR pending in Contiki about that topic, see https://github.com/contiki-os/contiki/pull/2098 , that should provide a more comprehensive fix, but I did not had time to look at it in depth yet. And I'm a bit reluctant to merge it into 6LBR blindly as it could stealthy break many things.

But if you're adventurous you could merge it and try if it solves your problem, in the mean time I will try to find some time to carefully review it.

title: tcpip_icmp6_call( ) problem in tcpip.c
body:
Hi Everyone,

I was recently having issues running my 6LBR implementation for long periods of time while connected to the internet. 

In the file, tcpip.c, there is a function tcpip_icmp6_call, which has a “XXX hack” message.

It seems as though for internet-enabled applications (as in the ping6 example), the icmp6_new function is called with NULL to initialize the uip_icmp6_conns structure.

However, after some amount of time, the memory used by “uip_icmp6_conns” is overwritten, causing the line: 

```
           “process_post_synch(uip_icmp6_conns.appstate.p, tcpip_icmp6_event, &type);” 
```

to throw a hard-fault on the MCU when an icmp6 message is received from the internet (i.e. NDP).

I have found that this is because “uip_icmp6_conns.appstate.p” is not a static object. When it is used properly, it points to a process and all that process’ properties. When this pointer’s target has been overwritten, the “process_post_synch” function fails, since the process it calls is some arbitrary memory location, not a process at all.

My solution is to move the declaration of uip_icmp6_conns from uip6.c to the top of tcpip.c, and add the “static” declaration modifier.

i.e. globally declaring the variable as:

```
            static struct uip_icmp6_conn uip_icmp6_conns;
```

instead of: 

```
            struct uip_icmp6_conn uip_icmp6_conns;
```

at the top of tcpip.c (the only file that uip_icmp6_conns is used in).

Additionally, in uip.h, the extern declaration of uip_icmp6_conns should be removed, since it is not even used in uip.h.

With uip_icmp6_conns set as a global static structure in tcpip.c (the only file in which it is used), the memory it uses will never be overwritten during the lifetime of the program, and therefore, when the internet-enabled application receives an icmp6 message such as an NDP handshake it will be able to run the appropriate process.

I have implemented this on my 6LBR and apparently eliminated the issues causing the hard-faults.

Thoughts?

Jordan

title: Dnsmasq conflict with systemd-resolved on Lubuntu 18.04
body:
Hi,

When launching start_flash.sh on Lubuntu 18.04, I have an error in the log file :
Dnsmasq cannot strat because address is already in use.

And effectively, the port 53 is already used by systemd-resolved.

To solve this problem, I had to edit scripts/setup.asp and add the following line to /etc/dnsmasq.conf, juste after interface=$WLAN 👍
bind-interfaces
listen-address=10.42.42.1

This allowes Dnsmasq to start on a different IP than systemd-resolved.

Fred

title: Handling Override off->on when triggered by EC
body:
## Description
It's possible that I'm misunderstanding the expected behavior, but I'm not sure the overrides are behaving properly. 

## Configuration
```yaml
entity_controller:
  closet:
    sensor: binary_sensor.0x00158d0003cc4255_occupancy
    entity: light.shelly1_2c76fa_relay_0
    sensor_type: duration
    delay: 30
    overrides:
      - sensor.foo
```
## Steps to reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Trigger motion sensor (light turns on)
2. Set override state (`sensor.foo`) to on

### Expected behavior
EC stops changing the state; the light that was on remains on forever.
(if the motion sensor was not triggered before `sensor.off` went from `off` to `on`, the light should stay off forever)

### Actual Behaviour
EC immediately shuts off the light
(if the motion sensor was not triggered before `sensor.off` went from `off` to `on`, the light does in fact stay off forever)

The idea of overrides is to stop EC from activating in the first place, which works correctly as shown in GIF below. I hadn't considered this case in the original design because it is not a use case of mine.

If EC is in **active_timer**, turning on an override entity will cause EC to exit **active_timer** and enter the *overridden** state. An unintended side effect is that the control entities are turned off, which is counter intuitive.

![103](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7984567/71256141-e98c1a00-236a-11ea-8efd-777a249841b7.gif)

The definition of **active** and all its substates is that the control entites are turned on when in that state. We could add a new state called **active_overridden** as a dirty solution. This then asks for equivalent states for **blocked**. is there a cleaner way to do this? What will fulfil the requirement?
I agree that the light state should be maintained as activating an override entity means "Leave the light the way it is and ceise further interaction with it"

[2019-12-20T13:52:31Z | mikeage | comment]

Active_overriden would probably work. Another idea might be to move the turn_off into the destination states (not, of course, including overridden). 

One caveat is that exiting overridden shouldn't go into blocked, I think. It's similar to the restart HA case, but probably more common.

I first assumed the former, but then it's really just a version of override with a built in time, so maybe you had something else in mind.

[I'm working on an implementation for the main issue here; it's actually seeming pretty straightforward, but I want to do some more testing before I share]

[2019-12-22T02:11:53Z | danobot | comment]
I guess constrained means EC is overriding itself. Override means some other entity is overriding EC. Checkt He readme, I think there's a description of each state. Seems very similar now that it think about it.

This component is about eliminating annoying things caused by dumb, basic automations. To stay true to that purpose, a light that is on when EC enters constrained should stay on. Is this easy to implement or are we completely breaking the state machine by doing this? Seems like EC state and light state are no longer congruent.

Just to be clear, I'm not proposing breaking EC (at least, I don't think I am; keep calling me out if you think I'm getting too far). What I'm trying to do is make it serve not just as a full control for lights (for which it's perfect as-is) but also as a replacement for the same automations if one wants to have lights that are usually automatic but also occasionally manually controlled. For example, in the bathroom, I always want the light to come on when I walk in. In the bedroom, I generally always want it during the hours when people are awake, but sometimes, I might want to nap in the middle of the day and so I want to tell it "ok, leave this off now". Conversely, there are times when I normally want it not to trigger, but in a few cases, I might want to say "keep this light on for now". And if/when I say "go back to pure automatic control", I don't want it to shut off and then turn back on from the motion that comes 1 second later. It's a bad experience, and it's bad for lights that are on smart relays (a smart LED couldn't care less, but a fluorescent fixture with a ballast really shouldn't be toggled like that).  But again, keep me in line if you think these are rather specific cases that don't scale out to others' applications.

[2019-12-22T09:05:49Z | danobot | comment]
We are on the same page, just coming up with a way to implement it :)
Did you see the `stay` option? theres a special state **active_stay_on**. once in this state, EC will remain on. 
You mention a lot of different usecases (too many to focus on in this issue).

title: DH returns 415 when no Content-Type header defined
body:
Please make Content-Type header non-required and use JSON request parser by default. Right now if you supply a valid JSON and no Content-Type the API will return HTTP 415. 

This seems to be redundant  on this stage jsut because JSON media type is used everywhere and there is no alternative media types implemented in DH. This will also help users who like accessing DeviceHive API directly (using curl or Postman or whatever)

This issue (or you may call this a feature :smiley:) is reproducible at least for Network POST method.

Error example:

``` js
{
  "error": 415,
  "message": "HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type"
}
```
comments:
[2015-10-24T21:50:22Z | mdolbin | comment]
I think we should not make Content-Type header optional for the number of reasons.

First of all it's not about having a some header string in a request. We need to explicitly check that sender wants to send exactly JSON string before we even try to parse it. 

For example, default Content-Type for POST request is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` which is used to send serialized HTML forms data. This means that the following code will produce the following payload: `command=command&parameters[prop1]=val1&parameters[prop2]=val2&parameters[prop3]=etc` which will cause JSON parsing error (assuming we are accepting all requests) on server-side and unexpected 500 Internal Server Error instead of code 415 with user-friendly error message:

```
$.ajax({
    type: "POST",
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/dh/rest/device/e50d6085-2aba-48e9-b1c3-73c673e414be/command",
    headers: {"Authorization": "Bearer 1jwKgLYi/CdfBTI9KByfYxwyQ6HUIEfnGSgakdpFjgk="},
    data: {
        "command": "command",
        "parameters": {
            "prop1": "val1",
            "prop2": "val2",
            "prop3": "etc"
        }
    }
});
```

Sticking to standards also makes it easier for us to integrate with new tools, libraries and applications.

On the other hand, it's a good idea to transfer less bandwidth. For example, we can return 415 code on parsing error. 

@demon-xxi @zubrabubra @SorJEF What do you think? Let's discuss and make some decision regarding this issue.

[2015-10-26T16:38:09Z | zubrabubra | comment]
I would go with defaulting content type to application json and then making it the only choice for now.  What are the reasons device would decide to send us data form encoded?

As from device perspective both json and form encoded are not native, while json accepted by human beings easily, and when someone looks on `command=command&parameters[prop1]=val1&parameters[prop2]=val2&parameters[prop3]=etc` he become disappointed with a fact that he needs to catch symbols in this spagetti :)

[2015-10-28T07:21:58Z | mdolbin | comment]
@zubrabubra What are the reasons device would decide to send us data form encoded?
I was talking about

> This will also help users who like accessing DeviceHive API directly (using curl or Postman or whatever)
> Majority of tools will use default Content-Type if it's not omitted. 

But yeah, from the device perspective it makes perfect sense to avoid sending redundant data.

[2015-11-05T15:00:01Z | YermakovSergiy | comment]
Checked situation with curl and with Postman (from chrome). Check in debug mode, showed that curl send header Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded and Postman send header Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8. I assume that the client generates a default Content-Type. And it can cause problems. Therefore, the header must be specified certainly. I propose to close issue.

title: Sending responses to Azure Service Bus via AMQP 1.0 fails after some time
body:
When connecting to [Azure Service Bus](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/service-bus/) via AMQP 1.0 from Ditto's connectivity service, after some time the Azure Service Bus seems to close the AMQP link (the connection stays open) or seems to no longer accept new links.
From that point on no responses can be sent to that AMQP address.

This was observed for *responses*. The *commands* are still received via another AMQP address - a "reply-to" address was specified for those commands via AMQP header, to which the response is sent.

Following log occurs in the log:
```
org.eclipse.ditto.services.connectivity.messaging.amqp.AmqpPublisherActor: Failed to send JMS message: [IllegalStateException] The MessageProducer was closed due to an unrecoverable error.
```

Maybe the Ditto connectivity creates too much links (e.g. when each "reply-to" is a new address, e.g. a UUID) so that Azure Service Bus prevents adding new ones.

title: closed AMQP 1.0 consumer after idle timeout is not restored
body:
Azure Service Bus has the behavior that idle AMQP 1.0 links are closed after ~10 minutes of idle timeout.

We get following log message and afterwards the AMQP 1.0 Azure Service Bus connection is in a strange state:
```
Consumer <org.apache.qpid.jms.JmsMessageConsumer@3b8f105d> closed due to JmsConnectionRemotelyClosedException: The connection was inactive for more than the allowed 120000 milliseconds and is closed by container '...'. [condition = amqp:connection:forced]
```

"Strange" because: after that message we get following messages:
```
May 23rd 2019, 06:56:14.973 Session closed: org.apache.qpid.jms.JmsSession@3230bc47 - Unknown error from remote peer
May 23rd 2019, 06:56:14.975 Connection interrupted: amqps://<...>.servicebus.windows.net:5671?amqp.saslMechanisms=PLAIN&transport.trustAll=true&transport.verifyHost=false
May 23rd 2019, 06:56:16.229 Connection restored: amqps://<...>.servicebus.windows.net:5671?amqp.saslMechanisms=PLAIN&transport.trustAll=true&transport.verifyHost=false
```

The last 2 messages repeat themselves each second.

We could/should react on `org.eclipse.ditto.services.connectivity.messaging.amqp.AmqpClientActor.StatusReportingListener#onConsumerClosed` and restore the connection.

What also can be seen: the default JMS client timeout seems to be 120s (see error message above) - we should increase that to at least 5 min.
Azure Service Bus' timeout seems to be ~9-11 minutes.

I'm not sure why this only happens on Service Bus - as for Eclipse Hono we also have consumers which are "idling" 2 minutes. Maybe the AMQP endpoint does however keep them open infinitely.

@kaizimmerm : could you please have a look on this?

collation-server      = utf8mb4_general_ci

title: DMF API: Cancel Download does not contain enough information
body:
I'm experimenting with the DMF API and I'm kind of stuck in implementing the Cancel Download workflow.

Right now, the CANCEL_DOWNLOAD message has no information about the "actionId" or "softwareModuleId" however the response (UPDATE_ACTION_STATIS) is supposed to have that information in the payload.

If I don't send a proper UPDATE_ACTION_STATUS response, then the CANCEL_DOWNLOAD message keeps being sent every time after a THING_CREATED message.

Any ideas?
comments:
[2018-02-22T07:23:23Z | michahirsch | comment]
Hi @ertanden 

there is actually the `actiondId` within the DMF AMQP message as `long` in the body of the message. Maybe not the best to just send the `actionId` as long in the body. 
The current message looks like
```
(
   Body:'2' 
   MessageProperties [
              headers=
               {    topic=CANCEL_DOWNLOAD, 
                    content-type=application/json, type=EVENT, 
                    tenant=DEFAULT, 
                    __TypeId__=java.lang.Long, 
                   thingId=dmfSimulated0}, 
                   consumerQueue=simulator_receiver
........
)
```

I guess there is missing the json-document in the body which should probably look like 
```
{
   "actionId" : 1
}
```

I'll keep this issue open as bug for the DMF cancel message body content to serve `application/json` instead of the just the `actionId` as long value because the `content-type: application/json` is actually set in the headers.

Hope this helps,
Cheers,
Michael

[2018-02-22T08:01:25Z | ertanden | comment]
@michahirsch Thanks for the reply, indeed it helps, so I'm not stuck now. 

I didn't realize that `actionId` was actually being sent in the body, I guess the documentation also didn't help because it didn't mention that (https://www.eclipse.org/hawkbit/documentation/interfaces/dmf-api.html).

Thanks for the hint and feedback.

comments:
[2019-01-10T13:38:49Z | kaizimmerm | comment]

[2019-01-11T08:21:20Z | kaizimmerm | comment]

title: Example device registry overwrites existing config when restarting in openshift
body:
The init container for openshift of the device registry copies the example configuration to the configuration folder using following command: 
`cp -u /etc/examples/example-credentials.json /var/lib/hono/device-registry/credentials.json && cp -u /etc/examples/example-tenants.json /var/lib/hono/device-registry/tenants.json`.  
However, this command overwrites the existing configuration. I think this is because the configmaps (example-credentials and example-tenants) are reacreated in the pod when it starts.  
This can be solved by replacing the -u flag with the -n flag resulting in following command:
`cp -n /etc/examples/example-credentials.json /var/lib/hono/device-registry/credentials.json && cp -n /etc/examples/example-tenants.json /var/lib/hono/device-registry/tenants.json`.  
From the [cp command page](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/cp.1.html):  
- -n, --no-clobber
              do not overwrite an existing file (overrides a previous -i
              option)
- -u, --update
              copy only when the SOURCE file is newer than the destination
              file or when the destination file is missing

title: Hono server continuously replenishes clients with additional credits
body:
When a client (e.g. a protocol adapter) connects to Hono in order to upload telemetry data or events it is provided with *credits* at the AMQP protocol level indicating to the sender (the client) how many messages the Hono server is willing to accept and process.
Hono itself gets credits analogously from the downstream container it is connected to (the Dispatch Router). However, Hono server erronously *adds* the credits it receives from the downstream container to the credits the client has been given which leads to a continuously increasing amount of credits being granted to the client.
Hono server needs to consider the (unused) credits already granted to the client when replenishing the client with credits received from the downstream container.

title: Fix encoding of OpenTracing span in AMQP messages
body:
My understanding is that the current encoding of OpenTracing information in AMQP messages could cause some issues it is not compliant with the AMQP spec.

About annotations the spec says (http://docs.oasis-open.org/amqp/core/v1.0/os/amqp-core-messaging-v1.0-os.html#type-annotations):

> The annotations type is a map where the keys are restricted to be of type symbol or of type ulong. All ulong keys, and all symbolic keys except those beginning with "x-" are reserved. Keys beginning with "x-opt-" MUST be ignored if not understood. On receiving an annotation key which is not understood, and which does not begin with "x-opt", the receiving AMQP container MUST detach the link with a not-implemented error. 

What seems to happen right now is that the `MessageAnnotationsInjectAdapter` is being used in combination with the `TEXT_MAP` format, which would directly inject `uber-trace-id` and `uberctx-*` into the message annotation map (see: `io.jaegertracing.internal.propagation.TextMapCodec`):

So it might happen, that a receiver simply closes this link when the annotation is present in the map.

The proposal would be to use something like `x-opt-opentracing-trace-id` and `x-opt-opentracing-ctx-` instead.
comments:
[2019-02-15T13:16:48Z | ctron | comment]
Looking into the code, it actually might be tricky to get the proposal implemented. Maybe a different way to do it would be to keep the current keys of `uber-*` but put them into the annotations under a single key, using an AMQP map.

[2019-02-15T14:24:28Z | sophokles73 | comment]
The `MessageAnnotations*Adapter` actually injects to/extracts from the AMQP message's *delivery annotations* at the moment. The naming of the class does not reflect this properly (bad :-1: ). However, this does not change the overall problem here.

[2019-02-18T12:58:10Z | calohmn | comment]
In general I think it's a good idea to keep an eye on the AMQP related work in https://github.com/w3c/trace-context/. There's a draft in https://github.com/w3c/trace-context/pull/217 there.
There it is proposed to use a binary format. As this doesn't seem to be supported by Jaeger yet, I guess it's premature to adopt it here.
In any case I think it would be good to also address https://github.com/eclipse/hono/issues/1012 when doing changes on the Adapter classes here.

[2019-02-18T15:00:24Z | calohmn | comment]
When following the approach suggested in #1012 (also trying to read the trace-context from the _application-properties_ of the bare message), it has to be noted that an AMQP map is not supported as value type there. I would therefore suggest using the plain property names (e.g. _uber-trace-id_) in the _application-properties_ case.

[2019-02-20T15:00:50Z | calohmn | comment]
Created PR #1054. 
I've opted for _not_ also trying to read the trace-context from the _application-properties_ of the bare message.
We can add such a feature later on when the w3c trace-context spec is finalized (and when jaeger has support for the binary format if that is used in the spec).

title: [User Guide] Examples for AMQP are broken
body:
The examples for AMQP in the User Guide are broken. E.g.:

`$ /hono/cli/target$ java -jar hono-cli-0.7-SNAPSHOT-exec.jar --spring.profiles.active=amqp-adapter-cli --message.address=event --payload='{"alarm": 1}'`

Here `--payload` needs to be `--message.payload`. 

And in

`$ /hono/cli/target$ java -jar hono-cli-0.7-SNAPSHOT-exec.jar --spring.profiles.active=amqp-adapter-cli --username="" --password=""` 

the arguments `username` and `password` need to be prefixed with `hono.client.`

Furthermore the application does not start with empty username or password.

title: Fix cache handling in RegistrationClientImpl (concerning multiple gateways)
body:
Relates to #930, #1093:
In order to support the scenario of a device connecting via different gateways (not at the same time but alternating between gateways), the caching logic concerning `assertRegistration` requests has to be adapted.

Scenario:
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-1` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked (last-via is updated), new cache entry with key `(assert, dev-A, gw-1)` is created
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-2` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked (last-via is updated), new cache entry with key `(assert, dev-A, gw-2)` is created
- device `dev-A` again connects via gateway `gw-1` => **cache hit** => assertRegistration is NOT invoked and last-via is NOT updated - that is an error

Possible solution:
When writing the cache entry `(assert, dev-A, gw-2)` above, we have to delete all other cache entries concerning `assert` and `dev-A`.

EDIT: We shouldn't cache `RegistrationResult` objects representing devices with multiple `via` entries at all (see below).
comments:
[2019-03-21T10:07:28Z | calohmn | comment]
Another possible solution: 
Use only `(assert, $deviceId)` as cache key in `RegistrationClientImpl.assertRegistration`.
When having a cache hit, check the cache value and the `last-via` gateway id in it. If it differs from the gateway id used in the request, retrieve the current registration information from the RegistrationService and update the cache entry.

[2019-03-21T10:16:47Z | BobClaerhout | comment]
I'm not familiar with the assertRegistration but if it can be compared with a database table I think I would create a table where the DeviceId would be the primary key of that table. If this assumption is correct, I would rather go for the second solution.
On the other hand: is it really needed to check if the id is the same, can't you  just always update the cache entry or is the update an expensive operation?

[2019-03-21T10:50:31Z | calohmn | comment]
Yes, the second solution is probably more straightforward.

> is it really needed to check if the id is the same, can't you just always update the cache entry or is the update an expensive operation?

Updating the cache entry is not enough, we have to do the remote call to the Registration Service and have the `last-via` property be updated in the device registry that way.
In order not to do that unnecessarily, the gateway id is checked. At least that was my initial idea.

But, thinking further about this, for devices with multiple `via` entries, I think we **always** have to do the remote call and update the `last-via` property in the device registry, because there could be multiple protocol adapter instances involved.
An example:
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-1` to protocol adapter instance `http-1` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to `gw-1`
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-2` to _another_ protocol adapter instance `http-2` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to `gw-2`
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-1` to protocol adapter instance `http-1` => regardless of cache content, remote call has to be done in order to set last-via to `gw-1`

[2019-03-21T11:17:21Z | BobClaerhout | comment]
> An example:
> 
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-1 to protocol adapter instance http-1 => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to gw-1
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-2 to another protocol adapter instance http-2 => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to gw-2
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-1 to protocol adapter instance http-1 => regardless of cache content, remote call has to be done in order to set last-via to gw-1

I think you have to assume that your cache is always out of sync. At the second action, `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-2` you will have to perform a remote call as well. I think the local cache is a rather dangerous concept in this case. The master of this data should be the device registry (and there will always be just one device registry, if not a syncing mechanism should be added here as well). So I propose to always request the data from the device registry and update the data in the device registry instead of keeping a local cache. This does not have to block the normal flow as it can be updated after the telemetry or event data is sent to the AMQP broker.

[2019-03-21T13:01:03Z | sophokles73 | comment]
The device registry implementation can control the caching behavior in the adapters by means of the *caching policy* which is included in all responses to *assert Registration*. The registry could, e.g. use the *no cache* policy for devices that are allowed to connect via multiple gateways and use the normal cache policy for devices that are only allowed to connect via a single gateway (or none at all).

title: Cannot deploy Hono 0.9 using Helm chart
body:
When trying to install Hono 0.9 using `helm install ...` as described in the deployment guide, Helm immediately fails, complaining about an invalid label value.

This seems to be the same problem as described in #491
comments:
[2019-03-21T14:04:39Z | sophokles73 | comment]
This problem will not occur when running the Helm deployment from master (because the version there is usually something like `0.x-SNAPSHOT` which is interpreted as a string instead of a number).

In order to use the Helm templates that are part of the 0.9 download archive, the following command needs to be run before running `helm install`:
```
~/eclipse-hono-deploy-0.9/deploy$ for NAME in $(find helm/templates -name *.y*ml); do sed -i -E -e 's/^(\s*version\:\s*)(.. \.Chart\.AppVersion ..)/\1"\2"/' $NAME; done
```
this will replace all occurrences of the `0.9` version label with `"0.9"`.

title: Concurrency issue while authenticating devices with SHA encoded passwords
body:
`MessageDigestPasswordEncoder` is not thread-safe as it uses the same `MessageDigest` instance for all `matches()` calls. However since `UsernamePasswordAuthProvider` executes password check within different threads this leads to wrong results and thus to failed device authentications. 

Possible solutions might be
- Use new `MessageDigest` instance for every request
- Use separate `MessageDigest` instance per thread
- Add some locking to `matches()`

If creating of `MessageDigest` is not an expensive operation option 1 should be easy and legit to implement.

WDYT?
comments:
[2019-04-12T15:18:47Z | sophokles73 | comment]
That indeed seems to be a problem. Thanks for reporting :+1: 

Creating a `MessageDigest` instance shouldn't be a problem. The time consuming part is invoking the *digest* operation where the hash is computed.
So, option 1 should be fine FMPOV.

Do you want to create a PR?

comments:
[2017-03-15T12:00:36Z | calohmn | comment]
The reason is the `System.in.read()` inside `waitForInput()` which is waiting for ENTER to be pressed.
As this is blocking, it is executed with `vertx.executeBlocking()` (so that is is run in a Vertx worker thread).

But although a Vertx worker thread is supposed to be doing longer-running tasks outside the Vertx event thread, these tasks should not run forever. To promote this, there is `VertxOptions.maxWorkerExecuteTime` (default 60s), causing warnings after this time has elapsed.

A simple solution to this would be removing the `waitForInput` method and letting the application be stopped by pressing CTRL+C ("Press CTRL+C to stop receiver.").
Cleanup work on shutdown can then be done in a @PreDestroy method.

(I would prefer CTRL+C also because it would allow pressing ENTER to add some blank lines in the terminal to better distinguish subsequent log output.)

title: Delivery outcome is always 'accepted' in northbound side while sending commands
body:
A northbound application sends a command to a device. The protocol adapter (tried with _MQTT_ and _AMQP_ adapters) sends back a _rejected_ disposition. This information is not cascaded to the northbound application and thereby the application waits until the time out expires.   

`CommandClient` implementation uses `AbstractRequestResponseClient.sendRequest(Message message, Handler<ProtonDelivery> onUpdated)` to send the AMQP messages. And the delivery state is always received as _accepted_ irrespective of the disposition sent by the protocol adapters.
comments:
[2019-06-14T08:03:35Z | calohmn | comment]
It looks like the reason is, that the CommandConsumer in the protocol adapter has `ProtonReceiver.isAutoAccept` set to `true` in its receiver.
Since the proper delivery update (with `rejected` outcome) by the protocol adapter is done asynchronously and not directly in the message handler of the receiver, the receiver will send an `accepted` disposition frame.

title: Error in DelegatedCommandSender while sending command to another adapter instance
body:
We get the following error in DelegatedCommandSender very frequently in our automated system tests (quote from tracing)

`{
  "key": "error.object",
  "type": "string",
  "value": "org.eclipse.hono.client.ServerErrorException: peer did not settle message, failing delivery"
}`

according log statement:

`peer did not settle message [message ID: DelegatedCommandSenderImpl-304, remote state: Rejected], failing delivery`

Our test does the following:
- Create new tenant
- Create new device
- Device connects to MQTT adapter
- Device subscribes to command and control topic
- Test waits for event that signals device is ready to receive commands
- Test sends command to device
- Test verifies if command was received by device

This sequence runs multiple times for the same device and we have multiple MQTT adapter instances running, i.e it is very likely that device is connected to different adapters during tests.

If we add a 1 second sleep between receiving event that signals device is ready to receive commands and sending of the command we do not get this error.

What do you think, can this be related to some timing issue in hono, or is it more likely that this is related to our messaging infrastructure?
comments:
[2019-08-26T09:06:27Z | sophokles73 | comment]
@calohmn can you please take a look at this?

[2019-08-30T05:33:26Z | calohmn | comment]
Adding some further debug output has revealed that the `Rejected` disposition has the error "Deliveries cannot be sent to an unavailable address":
````
Rejected{error=Error{condition=amqp:not-found, description='Deliveries cannot be sent to an unavailable address', info=null}
````
(I've improved log output since to always reveal this, see https://github.com/eclipse/hono/commit/7aa91cd29f3d16d0f28033c3de3bade16e09b753.)

What seemingly happened here:
The DelegatedCommandSenderImpl that forwards the received command on the device-specific command address uses a sender link on the *anonymous relay* (so that one link can be used for multiple tenants/devices).
That means the sender doesn't get credits for the particular address to be used here and so it isn't assured that there actually is a receiver for the device-specific command address.
The Qpid error message above indicates just that; no receiver on that address was available.

At first sight, this doesn't seem possible, because we always create a device-specific command receiver link *first*, before the application gets the indication that a device can receive a command.
But here the fact comes into play that a network of multiple Qpid dispatch router instances is used in this case.

So, the steps were:
The receiver link gets created in connection with Qpid instance A.
Then the command message should get sent on the anonymous relay in connection with Qpid instance B.
The information about the receiver link wasn't propagated in the router network to Qpid instance B yet, so an "unavailable address" is returned.

See also [this discussion](http://qpid.2158936.n2.nabble.com/Dispatch-Router-Anon-relay-sender-link-rejected-msgs-timing-issue-td7685763.html) on the Qpid list on this.

[2019-08-30T09:40:14Z | calohmn | comment]
To fix this, I see these options:
1. Insert a delay *after* creating the device-specific command consumer link and *before* informing the application about the fact that the device can receive commands. During this delay, the information about the attached receiver is supposed to be propagated in the router network, so that when sending the command message on the anonymous relay link, the message gets accepted (hopefully). 
1. Use a sender link with the device-specific command address (instead of using the anonymous relay). In case the received command has to be forwarded via the DelegatedCommandSenderImpl, the sender link is opened, the command message is sent and then the link is closed.
1. Use the current solution (with anonymous relay link) and do retries if sending the command message failed with the above error.

With solution 1, the question is how to choose a delay that is small enough not to delay the whole command processing too much (could be noticable especially in the HTTP case) but large enough to ensure qpid has propagated the receiver info to all instances.

With solution 3, the question is which delay period and which number of retries to choose.

I would prefer solution 2 here. I would rather have the (I guess small) overhead of creating the link each time instead of having to deal with delays or retries.

title: TTL unit assumed in seconds but AMQP 1.0 specification defines it in milliseconds
body:
The feature to set a default TTL for tenants is documented roughly in the example tenant json. [There a default TTL of `30` is set](https://www.eclipse.org/hono/docs/api/tenant/#tenant-information-format). I guess it was assumed that the TTL should be set in seconds as 30 milliseconds is most often not enough time to get a message through an AMQP network. However the AMQP 1.0 specification defines the TTL in milliseconds.
From the AMQP 1.0 specs:
>ttl time to live in ms
> Duration in milliseconds for which the message is to be considered “live”. If this is set then
a message expiration time will be computed based on the time of arrival at an intermediary.

So there are two possibilities:
* Either the unit in Hono has to be changed to milliseconds
* Or the TTL defined in the tenant json should be converted to milliseconds

In any case we should explicitly document the time unit which is used for the TTL.

title: Conceptual problem in connection handling
body:
To me it looks like we have a conceptual problem in the handling of connections to other services.

Every now and then, I recognized cases, where the adapters just don't become ready. And so I was digging into the issue. In the log you can then find something like:

~~~
2019-09-02T17:11:38.515Z INFO  [HonoConnectionImpl] stopping connection attempt to server [host: iot-device-registry.enmasse-infra.svc, port: 5671] due to terminal error
javax.security.sasl.AuthenticationException: Failed to authenticate
~~~

This "terminal error" will stop the client from trying to re-connect, and it seems like it never will re-try again. For as long as process is alive. So effectively, the process would be dead now.

My assumption was, that the pod would get cleaned up at some point, due to failing health checks. However that also doesn't seem to be the case. Taking a look at `org.eclipse.hono.service.AbstractProtocolAdapterBase`, you can see that the connections are checked in `registerReadinessChecks`, but not in the `registerLivenessChecks` method.

In that case, the "liveness check" would still always succeed.

Taking a look at the Kubernetes documentation (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-probes/):

> The kubelet uses liveness probes to know when to restart a Container. For example, liveness probes could catch a deadlock, where an application is running, but unable to make progress. Restarting a Container in such a state can help to make the application more available despite bugs.
> The kubelet uses readiness probes to know when a Container is ready to start accepting traffic. A Pod is considered ready when all of its Containers are ready. One use of this signal is to control which Pods are used as backends for Services. When a Pod is not ready, it is removed from Service load balancers.

It looks to me, as if the correct way to signal the "terminal error", is not through the "readiness" check, but through the "liveness" check instead.

Additionally, I would question the idea of a terminal error altogether. From what I see in our case, it has to do with an invalid service credential. So that problem will go away in a minute.

I think we should:

1. Trigger a liveness failure in case of a terminal error.
1. Event for a terminal error, allow to try again.

Fixing the first point is required to solve the issue. The second point would only allow the pod to recover itself, before it get killed by Kubernetes, and might be more of an improvement to the situation.

I also think we should fix this before 1.0.0!
comments:
[2019-09-03T07:19:48Z | ctron | comment]
Digging a bit more into the code, I think we could also fix the method `org.eclipse.hono.service.AbstractProtocolAdapterBase.startInternal()` in a way that the call to `connectToService` actually makes use of the returned future, and reports its failure to the startup chain. Failing the startup of the application.

[2019-09-03T08:19:15Z | sophokles73 | comment]
> This "terminal error" will stop the client from trying to re-connect, and it seems like it never will re-try again. For as long as process is alive. So effectively, the process would be dead now.

The behavior of the protocol adapters has been implemented this way deliberately in order to prevent useless connection attempts to services with which no connection can be established due to misconfiguration (on either the client or server side).

> It looks to me, as if the correct way to signal the "terminal error", is not through the "readiness" check, but through the "liveness" check instead.

I do not think that there is a right or wrong way here. We need to address two different scenarios here:
1. The service we try to connect to is implemented/configured correctly but is not (yet) ready for operation, i.e. it is in the process of starting up or we have temporarily lost network connection to it. In any case, once we are able to reach the service, a connection will be established.
2. The service is wrongly implemented or there is a configuration mismatch between the adapter and the service. This means that no matter how often we try to connect to the adapter, the connection attempt will always fail unless the configuration/implementation is fixed.

The first case is already covered by the current re-connect behavior. 

> Additionally, I would question the idea of a terminal error altogether. From what I see in our case, it has to do with an invalid service credential. So that problem will go away in a minute.

While the problem might be easy to fix (in most cases), whether it happens or not depends on an operator to become aware of it. I agree that with the current implementation this will be hard to detect as the adapter process seems to be running happily while in fact it doesn't try to (re-)establish a connection anymore.

> I think we should:
    Trigger a liveness failure in case of a terminal error.
    Event for a terminal error, allow to try again.

I am not sure what the second item is supposed to mean. But I would rather simply allow the adapter to try to re-connect in case of a terminal error instead of restarting the whole pod based on a failed liveness check, which is much slower and more costly.

FMPOV the readiness check is still the right way to make sure that
1. operators become aware of a problem with the adapter/service
1. allow the adapter to *auto recover* from the existing problem

The liveness check does not add much value here FMPOV because we would use it basically do the same as the HonoClient already does, i.e. trying to establish the connection once more.

However, the startup of the adapter does not need to depend on the successful establishment of the connections to the services because with the re-try behavior of the HonoClient, we already make sure that the connections get established eventually and the readiness check already signals to Kubernetes when this is the case.

[2019-09-03T08:29:05Z | ctron | comment]
> But I would rather simply allow the adapter to try to re-connect in case of a terminal error instead of restarting the whole pod based on a failed liveness check, which is much slower and more costly.

That is exactly my second point.

So reading through your explanations, I fail to see a reason for having a "terminal error" in the first place:

> Additionally, I would question the idea of a terminal error altogether.

Overall, still fail to see your intent here:

> FMPOV the readiness check is still the right way to make sure that
>
>   1. operators become aware of a problem with the adapter/service
>   2. allow the adapter to auto recover from the existing problem

When there is a way to "auto recover" from a "terminal error"? Then I fail to see the concept of a "terminal error".

Anyway, if your proposal is to simply ignore the "terminal" part, and continue re-connecting, then I am fine with that.

[2019-09-03T10:54:53Z | ctron | comment]
@sophokles73 Do you think #1473 is a better fix for this issue?

[2019-09-03T12:23:50Z | sophokles73 | comment]
> Anyway, if your proposal is to simply ignore the "terminal" part, and continue re-connecting, then I am fine with that.

That is exactly the proposal. We should no longer distinguish between terminal and non-terminal errors. With the backoff algorithm that @calohmn implemented recently, we should be safe to always try to re-connect, regardless of the underlying cause of the error.

@dejanb WDYT?

[2019-09-03T14:09:55Z | dejanb | comment]
@sophokles73 I think this is a move in the right direction, as there's no point in leaving pod running with the failed connection.

As for the liveness check, I'd still prefer to restart a pod if the reconnection logic is not successful in certain period of time. It might help with situations where process can pick up updated env and resolve the issue.

[2019-09-03T14:21:35Z | ctron | comment]
@sophokles73 So, I will move on with #1473 and simply drop the "terminal" stuff

[2019-09-30T14:10:09Z | calohmn | comment]
@selobosi Looking at the log file, the `cannot create concurrent command consumer` error comes *before* the AMQP adapter takes notice of the connection not being active anymore (`lost connection to device`). The period between the `STOPPING NETWORK` mark and the time that the adapter notices that is more than a minute. 
Have you tried setting the idle timeout when opening the connection to the AMQP adapter to a value lower than that?

The idleTimeout check that the AMQP adapter is doing on the connection takes both the idleTimeout advertised by the client as well as the local idleTimeout of the AMQP server (currently not set) into account. I think we should make the idleTimeout / heartbeat of the AMQP server of the AMQP adapter configurable to better handle situations like the above. 
Until then, you could try setting the idle timeout in your client.
As long as the idleTimeout check notices the inactive connection _before_ the device opens a new command consumer, just from looking at the code and the log output above, I think the above error shouldn't occur.

great analysis, @calohmn :+1: 

> I think we should make the idleTimeout / heartbeat of the AMQP server of the AMQP adapter configurable to better handle situations like the above.

It seems like the AMQP adapter also uses no default value, which would be used if the device didn't specify a heart beat in its open frame. So I think we should do both, define a default heart beat value for the AMQP adapter and make it configurable.

However, using an *aggressive* heart beat of several seconds only will increase network traffic in idle phases. This might be no issue for gateways connecting to the adapter but it might be a problem for constrained devices ...

[2019-10-09T13:32:22Z | unknown_author | comment]
Thanks for your analysis, @calohmn!

I configured an idle timeout in the client using `ProtonClientOptions.setIdleTimeout(...)` and `ProtonClientOptions.setIdleTimeoutUnit(...)` but why trying it out, I could not find a constant time between the initial successful creation of the command consumer and the connection to the device being lost - the longer I kept the device offline, the longer the connection took to be lost. It seemed like the lost connection always happened after the device came online again and after the concurrent command consumer was rejected.

@calohmn, you wrote
> The idleTimeout check that the AMQP adapter is doing on the connection takes both the idleTimeout advertised by the client as well as the local idleTimeout of the AMQP server (currently not set) into account.

Could you post a link to the line in the code where the two idle timeouts are taken into account? Maybe I can then better see how to adjust the client's idle timeout. Thanks!

[2019-10-15T06:47:15Z | sophokles73 | comment]
Ok, as it turns out, the AMQP adapter does not set an idle-time-out at all in its open frame, i.e. the AMQP adapter does not ask its peers (the devices) to prevent a timeout at all.
Given that the vertx-proton library only allows to set the (server side) idle-time-out value as part of binding the server to a port, we cannot use tenant specific values here but instead need to set a value at the adapter level.

@selobosi The idle time out handling is done in the [vertx-proton library](https://github.com/vert-x3/vertx-proton/blob/679fd2e2ca1d0d16eadd53a6fc2754c4c0056090/src/main/java/io/vertx/proton/impl/ProtonTransport.java#L220). However, I think that the explanation given in the AMQP 1.0 spec will be more helpful for understanding how this is supposed to work.

The way the AMQP adapter is currently implemented, it has little chance of detecting that the network connection to a device has broken down, so I consider this a bug.
Devices should also include an idle-time-out in their open frame in order to make the AMQP adapter send empty frames periodically if no commands are due for the device. That way the device can try to gracefully close the connection when it times out and then try to re-connect. If the connection was still alive at the time the device sent its close frame and the adapter actually received it, the adapter can then do its house keeping and close the downstream command consumer so that the device's next subscription request should succeed again ...

title: DEFAULT_TENANT is not created in local deployment
body:
**What I did:**
I followed the steps for the Helm based deployment (see: https://www.eclipse.org/hono/docs/deployment/helm-based-deployment/) on macOS using a Kubernetes cluster running in Docker Desktop.

**What I observed:**
The curl command for checking the existence of the DEFAULT_TENANT returns a 404.

**What I think what went wrong:**
The device registry could not process the payload example-tenants.json contained in the Eclipse Hono 1.0.0 Archive (see: https://www.eclipse.org/hono/downloads/)

**What I think may be a solution for the problem:**
With the implementation of the Support for multiple GAs in Registry and Tenant APIs (I think this is #623) the type of field `trustedCertificateAuthorities` in the class Tenant was changed from `TrustedCertificateAuthorities` to `List<TrustedCertificateAuthorities>`, see revision 3f4b120. The Unit Test runs fine, since its fixture in tenants.json does not contain a trusted CA, i.e. the change made was not covered by the unit test.

As far as I can see adapting the JSON in the unit test to contain a trusted CA and in the Eclipse Hono Archive to the changes made in 3f4b120 should fix the problem.

title: Demo certs cannot be used for PEM file based TLS configuration
body:
The demo keys included in the demo-certs module are ECC based (not RSA) and the corresponding key and certificate PEM files not in PKCS8 format. This prevents them from being used for configuring the Hono server based on the `HONO_SERVER_KEY_PATH` and `HONO_SERVER_CERT_PATH` because vertx only supports RSA keys in PKCS8 PEM files.

It would therefore be better to use RSA based keys and use PEM files based on PKCS8.

title: HTTP adapter: "message consumer already in use" error for TTD requests
body:
The HTTP adapter may get into a state where each new telemetry/event request with a `ttd` param for a specific device will fail to create a command consumer. Internally, a `message consumer already in use` is thrown because there already is a command consumer from a previous request that didn't get closed. 
This only gets resolved when the AMQP messaging network closes the existing command consumer link or if the adapter gets restarted.

Looking at a heap dump of an adapter instance that got into this state revealed that the command consumer didn't get closed at a particular HTTP request when there was an error creating the AMQP message sender (`not connected`).

title: HonoConnection.shutdown() blocks for 5s if called on event loop thread
body:
`HonoConnection.shutdown()` blocks the current thread for 5s waiting for the close frame from the remote peer.
If the current thread is the thread of the vertx context that the HonoConnection operates on, the response from the remote peer can't be processed while the thread is blocked, causing for the 5s timeout to occur.

Same applies to the `disconnect` method.
comments:
[2020-02-06T08:45:27Z | calohmn | comment]
IMHO, if called from (any) event loop thread, the `shutdown` method should not block at all. 
If the caller of the method wants more than fire-and-forget semantics, the `shutdown(Handler)` method should be used instead.

title: AMQP adapter: command response from gateway has wrong device id property
body:
When a northbound application sends a command to a device that is connected via a gateway, the device gets the command with a `reply-to` address that contains the gateway id instead of the device id.
When processing a command response message with that address, the AMQP adapter will then set the `device_id` property to the gateway id, not the device id.
This leads to the northbound application getting a command response message with the wrong `device_id` property value in such a scenario.

[2017-06-08T13:08:57Z | sophokles73 | comment]
The message in the log is the (failed) result of an attempt to authenticate a client (the protocol adapters I assume) by delegating to the auth server. This is probably due to the fact that the auth server is not (yet) up and running. However, because the protocol adapters try again and again to connect to the Hono server, the authentication request eventually succeeds and everything is fine. The failed connection attempts do not show up in the adapters' log by default.

I assume that the protocol adapters do work, don't they?

[2017-06-08T13:51:59Z | sophokles73 | comment]
I have taken another look and I believe that the client (the protocol adapter in this case) currently is not able to handle this situation because the `HonoClient` does not re-try on an authentication failure (which makes kind of sense because the credentials will not suddenly be correct on the next attempt). I think we will need to prevent this from happening by means of making the Hono server open its ports only once the services it depends on become available, i.e. the Dispatch Router and the authentication server.

[2017-06-09T07:58:48Z | calohmn | comment]
Yes, the authentication failure in the protocol adapter was indeed due to the auth server not being fully started yet.

Concerning the re-try: With the new setup of having an external Auth server, as it is currently implemented, an authentication failure doesn't necessarily mean that credentials are wrong - it can just be that the auth server is currently down.
Would it be possible to return a different error in that case (something like "service anavailable"), so that such an error can be handled with a re-try in the protocol adapter? 
If not, I would opt for an unconditional re-try or, as the adapter is in kind of dead state then, to shutdown the adapter.

body:

To reproduce:

=> this shows increased memory consumption

The heap dump diff shows additional `io.vertx.core.net.impl.NetClientImpl` objects (one for each connection attempt). They look like the main part of the memory leak.
comments:
[2017-07-13T13:39:16Z | calohmn | comment]
First thoughts:
The `io.vertx.core.net.impl.NetClientImpl` objects are still referenced in the `closeHooks` of the Vertx context.

To me it looks like there may be an issue in `io.vertx.proton.impl.ProtonClientImpl.connect()` / `connectNetClient()`.
The created `NetClient` instance is not closed there in case of a failed connection attempt. Thereby the instance is not removed from the Vertx context `closeHooks` and can't be garbage-collected.
If there is consensus on this explanation, we could file a vertx-proton issue for this.

I currently don't see a workaround in Hono. Letting the reconnects be handled by `NetClientImpl` (by using `protonClientOptions.setReconnectAttempts(-1)`) would undo the fix for #209.

[2017-07-14T07:50:33Z | sophokles73 | comment]
Your analysis looks very reasonable to me. I agree that invoking `NetclientImpl.close()` in the *failing* part of the connection handler in `ProtonClientImpl.connectNetClient()` should properly unregister the *closeHook* from the `Context` and prevent the memory leak.
Luckily, this seems not to be a problem when an existing connection fails as the underlying `ProtonTransport` will invoke `NetClient.close()` in this case.

> I currently don't see a workaround in Hono. Letting the reconnects be handled by NetClientImpl (by using protonClientOptions.setReconnectAttempts(-1)) would undo the fix for #209.

I also do not think that this would actually solve the problem because the `NetClient` is also not closed if the SASL handshake fails (e.g. due to incorrect credentials) :-(

Do you want to open an issue with the *vertx-proton* project or would you like me to do that? I can also create a PR since I am already *cleared* for contributing to Vert.x ...
